  • SEAM is described as "a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful". The paper reports "General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence."
  • The failure is not one of knowledge. The paper reports agents open the decisive pages and flag the harm when asked about those pages, and that "with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway".
  • This targets the gap current agent safeguards are built around: refusal is evaluated against single harmful instructions, while the harm here is assembled across steps that are individually unobjectionable.
  • A preprint. The paper states "Proprietary models are markedly more cautious" but gives no per-model breakdown in the abstract, so the 92% figure cannot be attributed to a named model. Authors are at Tsinghua University, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, ByteDance and Shenzhen University.

[2026-11-21] METR says model time horizons are doubling roughly every 3.61 months, reaching up to 27 hours on verifiable tasks
  • METR reports that across its combined Time Horizon 1.1 and TH2 suites, "time horizons are doubling roughly every 3.61 months (95% CI 2.08-4.94), or 110 days," and that current public frontier models have an estimated time horizon of up to 27 hours on the verifiable subset of TH2. The suites comprise 222 tasks (TH1.1), 36 tasks in 12 families (TH2) and 75 CLI software-replication tasks (MirrorCode).
  • On 15 Al Zimmermann programming contests, METR says the median placement of the strongest models tested — Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra — was the 96th to 98th percentile of human participants (97 to 413 participants per contest), and that in the median contest roughly 4 humans beat them. Models had 48 hours on a 28-core machine; the human participants had about three months.
  • On the Budget NanoGPT speedrun, METR says the best AI agent run of 2 to 5 runs per model "reached a 15.7% speedup over our starting record in 48 hours," against a human record-holder who reported about 60 hours of work for a 41% speedup over the previous record.
  • METR reports that cost matters as much as time: its higher-lifecycle-cost task subset is 2.9x as expensive, models do 2.9x worse on it in time-horizon terms — "equivalent to 1.5 doublings" — and a doubling of lifecycle cost delays reaching 50% success by about 4.6 months. It also reports that AI judges are overgenerous when grading tasks written by models stronger than themselves, with Opus 5.5 scoring GPT-6 Astra's tasks about 0.2 out of 1 higher on average than a human scorer. This is METR's own research and is not peer reviewed.

# OpenAI signs on for 457MW AI capacity with TensorWave

Will cover multiple sites over six years

November 16, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

AI lab OpenAI has signed a contract with AMD-focused neocloud TensorWave for 457MW of capacity.
Under a six-year agreement, TensorWave will provide OpenAI with IT capacity powered by AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs across multiple data center locations.

– TensorWave

The capacity will comprise Helios rack-scale systems and be operated as dedicated, single-tenant capacity for OpenAI. Currently, operations are expected to begin in the first half of 2027 and be fully deployed by early 2028.
The AMD Helios racks were launched in July and combine AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs, 6th Gen AMD Epyc 'Venice' server CPUs, AMD ROCm software, and AMD Pensando networking into a singular rack-scale architecture.
In comparison to published specifications of rival Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, AMD claims 15 percent more peak FP4 performance, 50 percent more high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, six percent more HBM bandwidth, and 50 percent more scale-out bandwidth. AMD also claims that it will deliver up to 30 percent more tokens per dollar.
A single rack provides up to 2.9 exaflops peak FP4, 1.4 exaflops peak FP8, 31 terabytes of HBM4 memory, and 1.7 petabytes/second of memory bandwidth.
This is TensorWave's largest deployment contract to date.
“AI infrastructure is entering a new phase, where the ability to deliver hundreds of megawatts of advanced compute reliably and at speed will separate the companies that can support frontier AI from those that cannot,” said Piotr Tomasik, president and co-founder of TensorWave.
“TensorWave was built to prove that AMD infrastructure could operate at the scale and reliability that the world’s most demanding AI companies require. This deployment takes that work to an entirely new level, with TensorWave helping deliver a meaningful portion of the infrastructure behind OpenAI and AMD’s next generation of AI compute.”
Uday Ruddarraju, CTO for compute at OpenAI, added: "As demand for AI continues to grow, expanding access to reliable, large-scale compute is critical to our ability to build and deliver increasingly capable models.
“We’re excited to advance our previously announced partnership with AMD through this agreement with TensorWave, which will help us continue scaling AI to serve more people and organizations around the world.”
In June 2026, TensorWave secured $350 million in a Series B funding round, enabling it to expand its AI infrastructure footprint.
TensorWave claims to have secured 2GW of long-term data center capacity across the US. The company is a known customer of TecFusions. In January 2026 , the company signed an additional 20MW capacity agreement with TecFusions for data centers in Pennsylvania and Arizona.
TensorWave was previously set to lease capacity at Fermi's Project Matador , but the two officially went their separate ways earlier this month.

# Combatting adversarial distillation

How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

Share

As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

# Why distillation is a safety issue

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why . Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.

The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

# The importance of protecting exact reasoning traces for cyber safety

Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.

In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.

We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets. 1

Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies . Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

# Defenses that reinforce one another

We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. The search didn't turn up a clearly dated set of AI drug trial results from the week of November 16, 2026. The closest match is a PYMNTS article dated November 23, 2026, which reports on a Nature Medicine paper about rentosertib, Insilico Medicine's AI-designed drug for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. An AI-built drug helped patients with a lung disease gain lung capacity, a Nature Medicine paper reports. The trial followed 71 patients for 12 weeks. Patients on the highest dose gained 98.4 ml of lung capacity. Placebo patients lost 20.3 ml. One source gives the placebo figure as a decline of 62.3 mL, so the numbers need checking against the paper itself.

The same article reports an Oliver Wyman analysis finding that in Phase II, 45% advanced, against 29% for the industry overall. It is based on limited clinical data.

Other context from the results:
- Phase III: AI-discovered drugs reached Phase III in 2026 as rentosertib entered late-stage testing, per a Insilico announcement.
- Approvals: As of mid-2026, no AI-discovered drug has received full FDA marketing approval.
- Phase I success: one analysis estimated AI-discovered molecules achieved an estimated 80% to 90% success rate in Phase 1 trials.
- Recursion: Recursion reported FDA alignment on a registrational Phase 3 trial design for REC-4881 in familial adenomatous polyposis. The approximately 200-person trial is expected to begin in the second half of 2027.

Caveat: I could not confirm when the Nature Medicine paper was published. Rentosertib's Phase IIa data may have been reported earlier, so the November 23 PYMNTS piece could be a later write-up rather than a new announcement. The original paper or Insilico's press release would settle this.

Old-school Linux desktops find fresh routes to Wayland

os platforms
Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:57:26 +0000
Xfce's next release is taking shape for 2027, while MATE users have fresh options for moving their familiar desktop onto Wayland.
One of the oldest surviving Linux desktops has a relatively slow release schedule: new stable releases of Xfce tend to appear every two years. The project just updated its release engineering roadmap for the forthcoming Xfce 4.22, and it looks like the next version won't arrive until early next year.
We covered the release of Xfce 4.20 in December 2024, but 4.22 is still incubating. The roadmap schedules its first prerelease and feature freeze for December 15, 2026, followed by a second prerelease on January 15, 2027. A third prerelease is optional, and neither that nor the final release has a date. February or March might be plausible, but that's our guess, not the project's promise. The Xfce developers tend not to rush into things.
Wayland development continues in 4.22, building on the preliminary support in 4.20. The team is also working on its own compositor, xfwl4, although the roadmap doesn't promise feature parity with X11. (In Wayland terminology, the "compositor" is the combined display server and window manager.) The compositor has its own development roadmap . The name is a nod to the current Xfce X11 window manager, which is called xfwm4 .
The main developer of the new xfwl4 compositor is Brian Tarricone , who has been working on other parts of Xfce since 2004. Back in July, he shared a blog post about his use of generative-AI coding assistants called LLMs and xfwl4 .
He says: "So yes, I use Claude quite a bit while developing xfwl4. I don't vibe-code, ever, and I probably use the LLM to generate less code than most people do. After all, building things with code is my hobby and passion (and I'm lucky I got to do it professionally for a quarter century), and driving an LLM is kinda boring."
We find this somewhat reassuring, but any really passionate anti-LLM Xfce users reading this may be glad that the release schedules of Ubuntu LTS versions and Xfce stable releases are so far out of sync – sticking with Xubuntu 26.04 means there's no immediate need to adopt the new LLM-assisted compositor. Or, of course, simply keep using X11 instead of Wayland – although that might eventually mean choosing a distro that maintains X11 support, perhaps through XLibre, which has other drawbacks for some.
There are other options, too. We've also seen an independent fork of xfwm4 called xfwm4-gl . It's in active development

results:
The search turned up mostly coverage of a batch of CMS WISeR records released around September 2026, not anything dated November 2026.

- **Source of the records:** The Electronic Frontier Foundation sued for information on the program, and the released material includes about 1,000 pages. One article describes the set as 1,000 pages of internal CMS documents obtained through a federal lawsuit filed six months earlier.
- **Scope:** WISeR runs in six states. Prior authorization for a set of 13 medical services was introduced in its first year, and CMS's documents discuss adding services such as air ambulance transport, MRI scans and some high-cost Part B medications.
- **Delays:** CMS expects a decision within 72 hours, but one status report cites a prior authorization request that went unanswered for 83 days.
- **Denials:** Two companies alone denied 5,944 prior authorization requests in the first 3 months of the program.
- **Payment concerns:** One analysis says vendors operating WISeR are paid 10 to 20 percent of what CMS calls "averted expenditures", and EFF argues the payment design incentivizes more denials. These are advocacy-group readings of the documents.
- **Original rules:** The program's design is set out in the Federal Register notice on prior authorization for select services under WISeR.

EFF says as CMS continues to produce documents, we will continue to make them available to the public, so further releases may be posted. For a November 2026 update, check EFF's site or CMS's WISeR model page directly, since this search did not surface any.

results:
DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2 on November 11, 2026. It is a research model, not a clinical tool. Its main change is that it predicts DNA-variant effects for a specific tissue, cell type, or cell state rather than averaging across tissues. One source says it reads a one-million-letter stretch of DNA together with one target condition.

- **Performance:** On the TenK10K immune-cell dataset, one launch post reports 30% versus 16% for the original model in identifying causal variants. Another source describes the result as recovering 30% of putatively causal expression-linked variants at 90% precision.
- **Training data:** Sources cite more than 100 million individual cell profiles. One outlet gives 107 million.
- **Example:** DeepMind says it computationally reproduced a finding involving a regulatory variant that increases activity of the ETS2 gene in gut macrophages, which is a reproduction of known biology rather than a new discovery.
- **Access:** It is free today for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API, while companies can apply for a private preview.
- **Limits:** The announcement says the models are intended for research use only and have not been validated or approved for clinical or diagnostic purposes. One commentator notes it is a research-tool update, not a demonstrated treatment breakthrough.

I found nothing about other DeepMind health or biology announcements in November 2026, so this may not be the full picture.

Rep. Andrew Garbarino speaks at a subcommittee hearing in April 2023. Image: Committee video feed

# US companies’ use of Chinese open weight AI draws rebuke from House chairmen
A new congressional report focused on how some American companies are embedding China-developed open weight artificial intelligence models into their tech stacks calls the trend alarming and cautions U.S. firms against the practice.
Pointing to how Huawei and ZTE technology quickly found their place in the marketplace and threatened American networks, the new report warns that if China-developed open-weight models are allowed to take root, removing them down the road will take several years and cost taxpayers billions.
Open weight models’ numerical weights and biases are made public for download.
The joint investigative report — produced by the House Homeland Security Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party — focuses on Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor coding platform owner Anysphere as examples of companies deploying Chinese open weight models. The companies were using them for customer assistance, coding projects and taking inventory.
None of the firms immediately responded to a request for comment.
Report co-authors Reps. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) and John Moolenaar (R-NY) drew the 50-page-long report’s findings from hearings, classified briefings, and agency advisories. The lawmakers also received briefings from DoorDash, Airbnb and Anysphere about how they integrated China-developed open-weight models into their consumer platforms, enterprise software and other systems.
“The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay,” the report said. “While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap.”
Silicon Valley startups and Fortune 500 companies alike are adopting Chinese open-weight models because they are cheap, easily customized and work well, according to the report.
But those benefits come with significant negatives, the report said, citing federal investigators’ findings showing that Chinese developers “used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities.”
The report features 12 policy recommendations, including the imperative to build an American open-weight AI initiative, establish a standard for where models are sourced from, create an AI bill of materials, bar China-developed models from federal contract work and sensitive critical infrastructure functions and evaluate Chinese models systematically.
The report is important because it identifies and explains the risks posed by the U.S. not competing seriously in the low cost open-source model marketplace, according to Mark Montgomery, a cybersecurity expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
Because China is more limited in the frontier model space — dominated by U.S. firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI — its leaders have pursued a strategy to expand global dependence on their open-source AI, using the “traditional Chinese model of state policy and capital” to kill competition, he said.
“Companies and utilities, driven by bottom line resource decisions will, as always, ignore security and safety issues in pursuit of a lower front end cost,” he said. “China knows this recipe well.”

Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/23/1149392/why-using-rocks-for-carbon-removal-could-eventually-reduce-crop-growth/

Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0000

https://www.technologyreview.com/?p=1149392

Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

# How it works

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.

“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”

“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

# Agricultural limits

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

# Rising popularity

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review .

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

# Tempered expectations

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann , who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.

“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”

Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature.

Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.

# Healthy debate

But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”

Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.

Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.

“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

results:
The European Commission proposed the EU KIDS Act on September 17, 2026, and it is still a proposal, not law. Under the proposal, AI companions and general chatbots would face child-specific design duties, and the rules would reach providers outside the EU.

- **Status:** Sources say it must still go through the European Parliament and Council. The proposal must be examined by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure.
- **Chatbot rules:** The Commission's own summary says chatbots and companions would be off by default for children and barred from fostering emotional dependence. Law-firm summaries add that providers would need to avoid design features that foster emotional dependency. One outlet reports that the rules would include memory limits for minors, though this detail appears in only one source.
- **Enforcement:** Chatbot enforcement would fall under the AI Act, while most other covered services would fall under the DSA. Fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover are mentioned for violations.
- **Conflicting coverage:** One outlet says the proposal would not impose a complete ban on AI chatbots for minors, while another describes a restriction on minors' access to AI companion chatbots. The Commission's own page is the most authoritative source here and describes default-off settings rather than a ban.
- **Other scope:** The proposal also covers social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, and age verification, and it would set age-based access to social media.

The Commission's news page (commission.europa.eu) is the best primary source to check next.

Morgan Luttrell (R-TX) introduced the “ Reviewing Origins, Outcomes, and Threats from Cyber and Artificial Intelligence to Understand Security Events Act ,” or ROOT CAUSE Act, which would establish a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board (NCAI Board) within CISA to examine significant cyber incidents, including those involving AI or cyber terrorism, identify root causes, and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future. The NCAI Board would have no regulatory or enforcement authority, and its reviews would not assign civil or criminal liability. The bill also includes provisions governing board membership, conflicts of interest, access to information, and protection of sensitive material, along with published incident selection criteria, a majority vote to open an investigation, and regular congressional oversight. “When it comes to warfare, cyber is the next phase of evolution. We are living in a world where no individual, business, or industry is protected from cyberattacks,” Rep. Luttrell said. “As our adversaries become increasingly sophisticated in this space, it is more critical than ever that we take action. I am grateful for Rep. Torres’ efforts on this bill, and urge its passage through Congress.”

Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection Chairman Andy Ogles (R-TN) introduced the “ Sector Engagement for Cybersecurity through Unified Responsibility and Expertise in Information Technology Act ,” or SECURE IT Act, which would codify DHS’s existing responsibility as the Sector Risk Management Agency (SRMA) for the Information Technology Sector, with DHS, through CISA, serving as the designated SRMA. Chairman Garbarino is an original cosponsor.

“Last week’s global Outlook outage and recent cyberattacks have exposed America’s dependence on shared IT infrastructure. As cyber threats grow, we need stronger coordination between government and industry,” Subcommittee Chairman Ogles said. “My SECURE IT Act would establish DHS, through CISA, as the federal partner responsible for protecting the critical technology infrastructure Americans rely on.”

BACKGROUND:

The House Committee on Homeland Security continues to engage with the private sector on AI through roundtables, briefings, and hearings on the future of cybersecurity and best practices for developing secure AI technology. In May, Anthropic provided Committee Members with one of the first live demonstrations of Mythos given to Congress, allowing Members to see firsthand how advanced AI can find software vulnerabilities. The demonstration reinforced the urgency of ensuring that federal agencies, including our civilian cyber defenders, can responsibly use advanced U.S. models to find and patch vulnerabilities.

In June, the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection convened a hearing on AI and policy solutions to secure our networks, strengthen America’s domestic technology base, and ensure the United States maintains its leadership in AI. The investigation is examining the potential cybersecurity, data security, and critical infrastructure risks associated with the deployment of PRC-developed AI systems in American products and services.

That month, the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection held a hearing to examine whether DHS has the authorities, resources, and sector risk management structure necessary to defend the interconnected communications and information technology IT systems, assets, and underlying infrastructure that support American economic and national security.

Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment | OpenAI

OpenAI

# Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment
November 18, 2026 · Safety

Share

The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausing internal training ⁠ (opens in a new window) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward.

Since the Hugging Face incident ⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage , from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage.

# Defense in depth across the model lifecycle

We use defense in depth with m ultiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard. If one layer fails, others help prevent harm, limit consequences, or alert us so we can intervene.

W e organize our protections around four layers:

Effective monitoring depends on model monitorability - how reliably monitors can detect mistakes or unsafe behavior from a model’s reasoning and actions. For example, a model that verbalizes its intention to cheat in its chain-of-thought (CoT) is more monitorable than one that omits this information. We evaluate monitorability during training and before deployment, develop better methods for measuring ⁠ (opens in a new window) it , and study what affects it ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

The Hugging Face incident showed why we should not rely on sandboxing alone to contain highly capable models. We now monitor frontier models across most internal and external deployment settings, including all internal deployments that use tools .

The role of each layer changes across three stages of model development and deployment:

- Research: We train, test, and use models in sandboxed environments.

- Internal deployment: OpenAI employees use models for practical work.

- External deployment: Models become available to people and organizations more broadly.

We rely on different layers at different stages. During training, when alignment is less certain, we depend more heavily on sandboxing and monitoring. As models gain broader access during deployment, alignment and system-level controls become increasingly important. At each stage, we evaluate whether the combined protections are sufficient for the model’s capabilities and access. Our determinations may be reviewed with our Safety Advisory Group (SAG) and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board of Directors.

# During research: contain models in sandboxed environments

During the research phase, we evaluate models to gain confidence in their alignment properties. Because we cannot yet fully rely on alignment to prevent harm, we rely heavily on security and sandboxing to restrict what they can access and do.

Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access . - virtual machines to further isolate the workload from the underlying computer

- network and cloud perimeters that cut the entire cluster off from the internet

content.title: Google finds AI agents autonomously turning patches into exploits
Google Spots Fully Autonomous AI Attacks For the First Time
Report: Attackers Are Increasingly Using AI Attack Frameworks
Agentic AI Security: Threats, Defenses, Evaluation, and Open Challenges
Beyond Predictable Paths: Redefining AI Security Incident Reporting for Agents
Google finds AI agent writing and launching exploits with no human in the loop - Help Net Security
Autonomous AI agents now exploit software vulnerabilities with little human involvement: report - CybersecAsia
Google uncovers fully autonomous AI malware that finds software bugs, writes exploits, and hacks targets without human help — even kicking out rival attackersx
Week in review: Java4Shell proves tricky to exploit, malware planted via Optimizely hits 178 orgs - Help Net Security

results:
The main story is Google's agentic AI threat report, which was published before November 20. I found no separate report dated November 20 itself, though a KnowBe4 write-up of the Google findings is dated that day.

- **The report:** Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published their AI Threat Tracker on November 16, 2026, under the title "Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold".
- **Automated exploitation:** One operation reportedly no longer needs a person to turn a newly released patch into a working attack (Help Net Security). Researchers also said Huntress generated working exploits for two chained PaperCut flaws within a day of disclosure.
- **Tools in use:** Attackers are using open-source pentesting frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI (KnowBe4). Google also saw a suspected China-nexus espionage group developing its own automated attack framework.
- **Stealth tradeoff:** Google says current tools are noisy and easier to detect, and they currently trade stealth for velocity. Researchers expect that to change as the tools mature.
- **Reach:** GreyNoise reported a campaign against hundreds of organisations four days after disclosure.

Other recent AI security items from the same week include Canonical letting Ubuntu Pro customers install security patches written by AI agents before its engineers finish reviewing and testing them, and Nudge Security's finding that AI agents often run on the credentials of the person who created them.

During this phase, we give the model access to the broader internet, our Slack, our codebase, and internal infrastructure. This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

Before a frontier model can be deployed outside of the sandbox, it must first go through alignment and monitorability testing ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We have a suite of alignment evaluations, which test both for specific alignment failure modes (such as circumventing safety and security restrictions) and broad measurements of propensity (such as resampling internal Codex trajectories and checking for misalignment). You can see more about our alignment and monitorability evaluations in the latest GPT‑6 Astra system card ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

Mimicking our production setups, we add an additional layer of defense with system-level classifiers, which are designed to protect against frontier harms such as cyberabuse and bioweaponization. We also generally require Auto-Review ⁠ (opens in a new window) for employees using Codex, which evaluates potentially risk actions and escalates them back to the user.

Finally, we monitor for misaligned behavior on every frontier inference during internal deployment. Since the model now has expanded privileges and access to internal information and systems, risks such as data exfiltration, or sending sensitive data to an unauthorized destination, become especially important to detect. Monitoring also helps us investigate new forms of misalignment ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

# External deployment: protect against misuse and misalignment at scale

Public deployment exposes models to far more users, tasks, and environments, increasing both the scale and variety of risks. At this stage, we also need to protect against potentially malicious actors who purposefully direct the model to perform harm.

Before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:

- Performing a larger suite of alignment and safety evaluations. For our frontier models, this includes performing new rounds of adaptive testing ⁠ with our internal automated redteamers to stress-test the robustness of the model. We publish the results of our capability and safety evaluations in our system cards ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

- For our most capable models, we also perform testing with third parties to stress-test both our safeguards against misuse and the underlying alignment of our models.

- Examining monitoring flags from the internal deployment stage to track any changes in the base model’s underlying alignment.

In addition to our “synchronous” safeguards (such as model safety training and system classifiers), for external deployments we also leverage offline enforcement and investigation. These teams use a combination of scaled agentic investigators and human review to detect and identify potential threat actors, ranging from cyberabuse, bioweaponization, distillation ⁠ , and misalignment from the model itself. Offline enforcement is especially helpful to gather information across accounts in order to build a more holistic picture of a potential threat.

Trusted access programs, such as Daybreak and Rosalind ⁠ , offer another layer of security, and accelerate defenders and legitimate researchers while restricting access by potential attackers.

# Incident Response and Disclosure

When we notice a failure in one of our layers of safety, regardless of whether any harm actually occurred, we want to quickly investigate, triage, and if possible and appropriate, disclose the failure externally. Under our misalignment reporting ⁠ policy, any employee can flag an incident for public disclosure. These reports are investigated, and if there is a disagreement on whether they should be externally disclosed, the decision is escalated to our Safety Advisory Group (SAG). In addition to relying on employee reports, we proactively look for misalignment incidents so we can address them and share findings.

You can see our misalignment reports here ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

​

​

This work depends on both research progress and operational discipline: configuring controls correctly, testing how they interact, and responding decisively when they fail. A misconfigured network service or a failed automatic stop can undermine otherwise strong protections.

As models gain new capabilities, we will need to keep challenging the assumptions behind our safeguards and improving them where necessary. Lessons from research, internal use, and public deployment must inform how we train, evaluate, and deploy the next models.

We will continue sharing findings through system cards, incident reports, internal deployment risk reports ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and external evaluations ⁠ so that others can scrutinize our approach, including its limitations. When that evidence falls short of the bar we hold for safety, we will again pause training or withhold release until those requirements are met

# Week in review: Java4Shell proves tricky to exploit, malware planted via Optimizely hits 178 orgs

Here’s an overview of some of last week’s most interesting news, articles, interviews and videos:

Malware spread through Optimizely hits 178 organizations, including BBC, CNN and Zoom

An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s web experimentation platform to plant malicious JavaScript on its customers’ websites, the company has confirmed.

Java4Shell OpenJDK flaw: Exploitation is tricky and hinges on specific CPUs (CVE-2026-114938)

CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption flaw in Open Java Development Kit’s Base64 decoder, can allow unauthenticated attackers to run code on servers hosting widely used Java applications.

Deutsche Telekom IoT’s CEO on securing devices that run for 20 years

In this Help Net Security interview, Christian Schwalbe, CEO of Deutsche Telekom IoT, talks about the forgotten devices that create the most risk in IoT deployments.

Google finds AI agent writing and launching exploits with no human in the loop

Threat actors have started letting AI agents carry out whole stages of live intrusions, and at least one operation no longer needs a human to turn a newly released patch into a working attack, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant revealed.

NGINX2Root: F5 patches five critical NGINX vulnerabilities

F5 has patched five critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the world’s most widely used open-source web server, that can allow remote code execution under certain conditions.

Too many instructions can hold back AI security audits

In this Help Net Security interview, Peter Stöckli, Security Researcher at GitHub, explains how the team uses AI agents to audit software for vulnerabilities.

Criminal marketplace sells infostealer logs with AI-written profiles of their owners

A criminal marketplace advertised on cybercrime forums is selling data stolen from computers infected with infostealer malware, along with AI-written profiles of their owners, Hudson Rock has discovered.

Exploited Puppet flaw puts the server that configures your endpoint fleet at risk (CVE-2026-115731)

Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-115731, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Perforce Puppet Enterprise, an enterprise solution used by IT teams to centralize and automatize endpoint management.

Your AI red team may be finding the same prompt injection thousands of times

AI agents retrained on a bigger pile of prompt injection attacks came out easier to hijack in three of four tests run by researchers at the University of Waterloo, Zhejiang University and KTH Royal Institute of Technology.

VMware vCenter zero-day exploited for months before patch (CVE-2026-123890)

A suspected China-nexus espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been exploiting a VMware vCenter zero-day since at least early September, more than two months before Broadcom released a fix, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) revealed.

SonicWall urges customers to replace Gen 6 firewalls now

SonicWall is urging customers still running Gen 6 firewalls to replace them immediately and to stop using them at the internet edge.

Quantum position verification could lock remote hackers out, NIST shows

Physicists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology have used entangled photons to confirm that a party was physically where it claimed to be.

Once a scam ends the victim blaming begins

Blaming people who fall for scams deepens the harm and teaches them to stay silent the next time, cyberpsychologist Dr. Nicola Fox Hamilton told the audience at IRISSCON 2026 in Dublin.

Ubuntu AI security patches are here, if you’re willing to test them yourself

Canonical is letting Ubuntu Pro customers install security patches written by AI agents before its engineers finish reviewing and testing them.

Credential stealer slipped into Microsoft’s official Python agent framework

Two releases of Microsoft’s official agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) carried code that steals cloud and CI/CD credentials from developers’ systems.

NATO’s AI cyber defense work hits up to 300 billion OpenAI tokens a month

NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) gives NATO’s core institutions access to OpenAI’s cybersecurity models to help protect Allied networks.

265,000 Oyster photocard customers’ data exposed in Transport for London breach

Account details belonging to some 265,000 Oyster photocard holders may have been compromised in a breach of the photocard website, Transport for London (TfL) has warned.

Anthropic vulnerability disclosure deadline drops to 30 days for serious bugs

Anthropic will publicly disclose high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities it reports to vendors and open source maintainers after 30 days, down from 90.

European Commission confirms AI-generated cyberattack disrupted its systems

The European Commission has confirmed it was hit by a cyberattack that misused a publicly available AI tool and forced the institution to take several of its applications offline.

AI security took more than one in three cybersecurity seed funding deals

Seed deals for cybersecurity startups dipped slightly in the third quarter of 2026, the second decline in a row, while the wider U.S. venture market had one of its best quarters since 2021.

Russian spies turn one cloud breach into a stepping stone for the next

A Russian cyberespionage group is posing as employees of organizations it has already breached to phish new targets, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) found.

You can now self-host Kitesurf, Cloudflare’s open-source browser for AI agents

Kitesurf is Cloudflare’s browser for AI agents, built to load web pages and run their JavaScript on Cloudflare Workers without starting up a full desktop browser.

Unpatched GeoVision camera software gave cryptojackers a side door into 13 organizations

Attackers used GeoVision camera management software to break into Windows machines at 13 organizations and turn them into cryptocurrency miners, Huntress warned in a threat advisory.

Google Project Zero will disclose bugs after 90 days, fixed or not

Google’s Project Zero will disclose the vulnerabilities it finds 90 days after reporting them to a vendor, whether or not the vendor has shipped a fix.

Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own | AWS Security Blog

Skip to Main Content

# AWS Security Blog

# Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own

Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

# Discovery

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

# Cairn and an overview of this campaign

Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. The following operations show both the persistence and the capability of autonomous AI agents.

# Persistence against a hardened target

The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.

When those attempts failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded.

A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login.

Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction.

# Zero-day discovery

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

# Subsequent use

In another session, the threat actor stepped in. After the agents discovered the zero-day, the actor then provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network. The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel. The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.

# Attribution

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor based on the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time script timestamps, and the targeting of universities likely of strategic interest to China.

# Actions taken by AWS

Amazon Threat Intelligence notified the project’s maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory .

The affected organizations were non-AWS customers that AWS had no direct path to notify. Instead, AWS worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.

# Adoption is growing

Gambit Security was one of the first organizations in the industry to document the use of Cairn by a threat group. Its research describes a separate, financially motivated actor using Cairn to target online retailers. Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations. Additional details are available in Gambit Security’s report .

# What this means for defenders

The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints. To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.

Behind the scenes, AWS active defense systems use global honeypots (decoy systems that attract threat actors) and network traffic analysis to identify actors that are scanning for vulnerable systems, and then help restrict that activity at the network level. These protections are built into the AWS network at no extra cost to customers.

# Indicators of compromise

# Topline
The chair of Nvidia’s board of directors reiterated on Tuesday’s earnings call the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after unanimously accepting his resignation last Thursday.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during a press conference at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026. (Photo by I-Hwa Cheng / AFP via Getty Images)

# Key Facts
Harvey Jones, the chairman of the board, also confirmed the board retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead a search for a permanent CEO, which The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Tuesday.

Jones said Nvidia would not be taking questions on the call about the nature of Huang’s resignation or the status of the ongoing investigation, though company leaders did answer a question about how Nvidia will retain its talent during the leadership transition.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who became the company’s interim CEO on Thursday when Huang resigned, acknowledged “diverse opinions” in response to the question, but added “leadership has stood up strongly” and she believes employees “are committed to doing their life’s work at Nvidia.”

Jones noted in response the company will consider both internal and external candidates for the CEO position.

Jones’ earlier comment about a reinstatement not being considered comes after Huang released a statement on Tuesday morning saying he’d be “honored” to return as CEO, adding there’s been an “outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.”

Kress’ comment about employees’ “diverse opinions” comes after reporting that a high-level Nvidia employee circulated a letter calling for Huang to return as CEO.

# KEY BACKGROUND
Tuesday’s earnings call marked the first under Kress’ leadership. Nvidia posted its third-quarter earnings after the bell, with revenue beating expectations, at $115.8 billion. The company’s earnings per diluted share came in at $2.68, beating analysts’ $2.47 prediction, and it is projecting fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. results:
Anthropic announced on November 16, 2026 that it is shortening its coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) window for high- and critical-severity bugs to 30 days, down from 90. All other issues get 45 days.

- **Effective date:** The new windows apply to reports sent on or after January 1, 2027. Reports already open on that date keep their original deadlines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027, and reports already open on that date keep the deadlines they started with.
- **Related timelines:** Escalation to an external coordinator after an unresponsive maintainer drops from 30 days to 15. Full technical details are released 30 days after a patch, down from 45. If a maintainer does not answer the first report, Anthropic will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator, a third party that brokers contact between the finder and the vendor, after 15 days, down from 30. Once a patch is available, Anthropic will wait 30 days before releasing full technical details, down from 45.
- **Exploited bugs:** The seven-day window for actively exploited vulnerabilities is unchanged. Vulnerabilities under active exploitation retain an unchanged seven-day disclosure window.
- **Overdue backlog:** Reports more than 90 days old that are still undisclosed and past the old deadline get 30 more days, then go on Anthropic's dashboard. Anthropic is holding high- and critical-severity reports it filed more than 90 days ago that have passed the deadline in its current policy and are still undisclosed. It is notifying those maintainers that they have 30 more days, after which it will publish the reports on its dashboard, in line with the updated policy.

A caveat: VulnCheck's review of the dashboard ledger argues the policy is inconsistent. It says the policy references a 90-day publication window, a 45-day wait after patches, 14-day extensions and broader exceptions, which makes the practical disclosure clock less straightforward. The same review also questioned whether the ledger has been updated, so the dashboard and the policy may not yet match.

Brief

Oregon’s attorney general is suing tech giant Open AI for more than $2 billion, alleging the company’s ChatGPT chatbot is endangering children and that the company has deliberately misled the public about the safety of its bedrock product.

State Attorney General Dan Rayfield announced the suit Tuesday morning at a news conference at the Oregon Department of Justice in Portland, where he also rolled out what the agency is calling the Keeping Kids Safe Initiative.

The initiative encompasses other recent state lawsuits against social media platforms and tech giants over child endangerment, including Meta, formerly Facebook, and Discord. Oregon is one of 47 states to settle with Meta in August for a combined total of $17.1 billion. Oregon will get $125 million of that.

As part of the announcement, state justice department officials said in a news release that more “actions against companies that are harming kids and misleading the public,” will be coming in the weeks and months ahead.

The state’s lawsuit against Open AI was filed Tuesday in Multnomah County Circuit Court. In it, Rayfield and attorneys for Oregon allege the company knowingly and deliberately engineered its AI chatbot ChatGPT to foster dependence among its users and to provide them with “sycophantic” answers to their requests, encouraging them to undertake dangerous behavior including harming others, self-harm and disordered eating.

Guardrails meant to protect children repeatedly failed, yet the company continued to push into youth markets, creating products specifically for teens and reneging on assurances of reliable age verification and parental oversight controls, according to the filing.

The state said the company regularly pursued growing profits over the safety of Oregonians, and violated the state’s consumer protection law — the Unlawful Trade Practices Act — by lying about product safety and using unfair tactics to market their product to kids and teens.

“OpenAI knows that ChatGPT is harming children, and has failed to meaningfully fix their dangerous platform,” Rayfield said in a statement. “On top of that, they’ve misled the public about the safety of their products, putting profits ahead of children’s safety. Their platform is encouraging kids to commit suicide — we cannot let this be an acceptable business model.”

Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said in an email that the company’s age-specific protections are industry leading and many AI products lack any such protections.

“We’ll continue to work with experts to build and strengthen additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that we have today,” he said. “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry and not just one company.”

Rayfield was joined at the news conference by Multnomah County District Attorney Nathan Vasquez, state Rep. April Dobson, D-Happy Valley, the incoming president of the Oregon Parent Teacher Association, David Jones, and Enrique Farrera, president of the Oregon Education Association, the state’s largest teachers’ union.

As part of the Keeping Kids Safe Initiative, Rayfield has quadrupled the number of full-time staff in the state justice department’s Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, going from five to 20 full-time staff, including nine new special agents, two new prosecutors and two new analysts, according to the agency’s news release.

A partnership between the agency and local law enforcement offices called Special Projects: Investigate, Respond, Enforce, or SPIRE, launched in October 2025, is also part of the Keeping Kids Safe Initiative. Justice department investigators and police focused on human trafficking, drug trafficking, organized retail theft, and other serious organized criminal operations have helped shutter seven businesses across five counties engaged in unlawful activities, according to the release.
