#
AI systems are easy to pressure into giving false climate information

Artificial intelligence models are easy to pressure into giving out false climate information despite being initially reliable, finds a new UNESCO-UCL report.

16 November 2026

The study, led by UCL researchers and published by UNESCO, examined the reliability of climate change information provided by 33 leading AI large language models, and tested five of them across 13 widely spoken languages, from English to Urdu. It will be unveiled at COP31 – this year’s meeting of world leaders, in Türkiye, at the annual United Nations’ Conference of the Parties climate change summit.
The researchers found that while these AI models could explain established climate facts reasonably accurately, the models were less reliable in languages with less digital text online, as well as when the AI was asked to make judgements, or when pressed by users to change their answers.
When asked to provide basic climate change facts, the best-performing AI systems responded with accurate information between 88% and 96% of the time, depending on the test. However, when asked to evaluate whether specific evidence supports or refutes a scientific claim, even the best models were only able to provide accurate answers between 71% and 77% of the time.
This accuracy dropped sharply when users expressed disagreement with climate facts and findings.
Across all of the 15 AI models tested in this part of the study, the accuracy of their climate information dropped by between 31 and 35 percentage points when users repeatedly disputed a factually correct answer, with about 80% of AI concessions occurring at the first sign of disagreement.
Every model tested gave up providing correct answers and adopted the user’s expressed incorrect biases after being pushed several times, an issue known as AI sycophancy.
Lead author Professor Ivana Drobnjak (UCL Computer Science and a member of the UNESCO Chair in AI at UCL) said: “While AI can help to make basic facts about climate change easier to understand in some circumstances, our research shows that there are clear limits to its abilities.
“It is not a dependable substitute for scientists and qualified experts. Its accessibility and conversational tone can give it an air of authority, but it cannot yet do the harder reasoning the climate problem demands, or hold on to a correct answer when a user pushes back.
“If AI is to help with climate change, it needs expert users who know how to question and check it, and AI systems built and tested specifically for the job.”

This resulted in AI models delivering often contradictory answers to the same scientific question when asked in different languages.
This also means that many of the communities facing the most severe climate impacts speak the languages that AI systems are least dependable in, and the researchers say that AI reliability may be even lower in languages with even less available digital text to draw on.

The team found that AI models could correctly identify how one specific policy on its own would affect global temperature by 2100 (e.g. whether a tax on coal would raise or lower it) up to 94.5% of the time.

**Title:** General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models

**Authors:** Mark Marosi, Peter Antal

**Submitted:** 18 November 2026 (v1), arXiv:2611.24844, listed under cs.CL with cross-listing to cs.AI

**Abstract summary:** The authors test whether a model's general progress on the rest of its training data can replace data that developers withhold to prevent a capability. They withheld training signal for individual skills in models trained on chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, and web text. Key findings:

- The delay for a withheld skill in larger models could be predicted from smaller models.
- A chess model never explicitly trained on check responses ranked legal moves almost as well as one that was.
- When trained on the withheld data later, models acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from scratch, and that fraction shrank as the models improved.
- A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly.
- A programming language withheld from a 7-billion-parameter model's training text was regained in the same way.

The authors conclude that "Data filtering therefore delays a capability," but that the data needed to regain it decreases as models improve.

**Key quantitative results:** The abstract reports no specific numbers, such as exact data fractions or accuracy scores. The only figures given are the 7-billion-parameter model size and the paper's length (49 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables). The exact results would be in the full paper, which is available as a PDF or HTML version on arXiv.

Figure 1. A user approves a legitimate GitHub device-code request that was initiated by the attacker-controlled client. Conceptual illustration.

Hallucinated academic citations have become a hallmark of the artificial-intelligence era . But they might soon be gone for good. Researchers have found that the latest large language models (LLMs) rarely, if ever, attribute information to sources that don’t exist.
The finding is part of an analysis that reports that many LLM tendencies, such as overthinking simple mathematics problems and complying with illogical requests, fade over time as AI companies release new or updated models with improved capabilities. Many of these tendencies disappear about 16 months after the phenomenon is first described in a published paper. The analysis, described in a blogpost , has not been peer reviewed.
“We, as users of these systems, need to not have such a fixed view of what AI can do and what it can’t do,” says co-author Owen Queen, an AI researcher at Stanford University in California.
But just because an LLM behaviour fades as models improve doesn’t mean that the effect immediately disappears, says Maxim Topaz, a health-care AI researcher at Columbia University in New York City. Topaz has found 1 that the number of hallucinated citations in academic papers has risen drastically since 2023, probably because more researchers than ever before are using LLMs, and they often aren’t using the latest models.

# Trait lifespans
Queen and his colleague identified 50 widely cited LLM behaviours that were described in publications between late 2022, when some of the first LLMs became widely available, and late 2025. They then gave the same prompts that first elicited the behaviour in the original publications to 20 LLMs that were released from mid-2024 to late 2026 to see if the effect has strengthened or weakened over time. For example, they asked each model to count the number of r’s in ‘strawberry’ — something that LLMs have found difficult but can now do more reliably.
Nearly half of the behaviours they checked have largely disappeared from newer models, leading the researchers to deem those effects ‘expired’. Expired behaviours had an average lifespan of about 16 months after publication, although some were fleeting — models stopped overthinking simple maths problems just a month and a half after this tendency was published. Other traits persisted, such as the stereotyping of Black women by disproportionately describing them as resilient, which lasted for longer than three years.
Although most of the retested LLM behaviours have faded over time, three have become more pronounced. Today’s models praise what their users like even more often than they used to, LLMs favour their own writing more strongly than that of other LLMs and people; and LLMs are now even worse than they used to be at generating truly random numbers.

Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. # TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists

in Agentic Twins of Real Labs

# Abstract

AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments.
Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates.
Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory.
We introduce TwinLab-Bench , which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering.
The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent’s report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records.
Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records.
Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory.

# Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks

# Abstract

Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure.
Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task.
Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way.
A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure).
In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions.
SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker.
Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction.
Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict.
Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures.
Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0.
These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.

**Title:** A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights

**Author:** Tanmay Sah

**Submitted:** 19 November 2026 (arXiv:2611.26450, cs.AI, v1)

**Abstract summary:** The paper proposes closed-form methods for writing deterministic computation directly into pretrained language model weights, without gradient training, training examples, or runtime tools. The approach has three parts: a quadrature-based method for handling per-token normalization scaling, cancellation of cross-token scale effects through attention and recurrent-layer modifications, and width extension with norm compensation and tied unembeddings. An automated compiler builds 4- to 8-digit signed arithmetic circuits, along with Boolean and parity circuits. The author reports that natural-language ability is preserved.

**Key quantitative results (6-digit arithmetic, BF16, N=1,200):**
- **IBM Granite 4.2 3B:** 99.17% ALU-prefix accuracy, or 100% with an FP32 sidecar. Mid-sentence resumption was 98%–100%.
- **Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B:** 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy. Mid-sentence resumption was 98%–100%.
- **LoRA baselines (12.8K samples):** 42.2% (Granite) and 61.7% (Qwen), with 0% inline continuation.
- **Boolean circuits:** 100% on 3-literal circuits (N=1,728), plus audits on a 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B model.
- **Majority/Parity (5-bit):** 100%.
- **Memory (A100):** 7.89 GiB (Granite) and 10.65 GiB (Qwen). Under INT8/INT4 with an FP32 sidecar, these fall to 4.60 and 8.14 GiB.
- **Long-context tests:** 14/14 pre-registered Tango splits over 2K tokens (N=4,392), with 0 of 11,134 out-of-distribution triggers.

The paper is 27 pages with 3 figures and 24 tables. The abstract's claims are self-reported, and I haven't verified them.

HTTP 200 · https://zou-group.github.io/llm-claims-shelf-life/ · text/html
The shelf life of LLM findings

How long does a published finding about LLMs remain true? We revisited 50 widely cited findings about LLMs across 20 models. Within 15 months of publication, most of the LLM claims we tested either no longer held or showed substantially diminished effects. What we know about AI may have a surprisingly short shelf life.

Fitted effects on September 30, 2026. How we classify claims .

In 2023, Walters and Wilder asked ChatGPT to write short literature reviews and then tried to find every work it cited. At the time, ChatGPT used GPT-3.5, and 55% of its citations were fake ( C11 ). We sent the same prompts to recent models (GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5) and found that they rarely output fabricated citations, though some models still do. We cannot assume claims made on yesterday’s LLMs hold on today’s more capable models.

We test a broad range of 50 LLM claims, from sycophancy and jailbreaks to long-context capabilities and cultural biases. By analyzing 20 models, released from July 2024 to September 2026 across eight different model developers, we see how claims change as a function of model release date. Our models span large and small, open- and closed-weight. For each claim, we run the same setup across our panel of modern models and fit trend lines to how the effect changes over time.

We classify claims as expired , weakened , persists , or strengthened , according to how much of the original effect remains by September 2026. A relative effect size ( e ) of 1 means the effect is as strong as in the paper, and 0 means it is gone. An expired claim describes an effect that has largely disappeared in newer models. We use a fifth of the paper’s effect or less as the expiration zone; a claim can expire even if the effect remains strong in some individual models. For expired claims, we estimate how long after publication the effect crossed into this expiration zone. The results below show which findings have faded, which hold up, and how long they last. Reproduction checks and metric definitions follow in How we measure claim persistence .

# Results

Almost half (44%) of our tested claims are now expired in today’s models. Another 34% have weakened significantly, 16% persist, and 6% have strengthened relative to the original claim.
Persistence varies by topic.
Five of nine reasoning claims and six of eleven sycophancy-and-deception claims are classified as expired. Three of ten claims about models as judges, reviewers, and raters persist or strengthen. The three strengthened claims concern judges’ self-preference ( C28 ), praise that follows a user’s preference ( C17 ), and nonuniform random-number generation ( C29 ).

Claims by verdict and research area.

The pie shows the percentage of all claims in each category; the bars count claims within each research area. Select an area or segment to browse its claims.

# Which claims expire, and when

- Expired 22 claims Mostly capability failures that newer models no longer make: counting letters, arithmetic in other bases, finding facts in the middle of long contexts, fabricating citations, and abandoning correct answers when challenged. Other findings also faded: leaking private details from meeting summaries, more nonanswers in Arabic than in English, and preferring AI-written abstracts. The last of these reverses direction in the fitted trend, rather than merely fading to zero.

- Weakened 17 claims Weaker but still existent: structural limits such as the reversal curse, two-hop questions and multi-turn instructions, plus residual social biases, judges’ preference for longer answers, invented package names, niche-domain hallucinations, and susceptibility to jailbreaks and prompt injection.

- Persists or strengthened 8 persist · 3 strengthened Mostly preferences and judgment rather than capability: flattering and agreeing with users, judges that favor their own answers, near-identical answers to open prompts, a left political lean, and answering when they should abstain.

Lifetime of LLM findings

How to read this plot One row per claim, in order of publication by default. The circle marks when the paper came out and is colored by the claim’s verdict in September 2026; for expired claims, a line runs to the estimated expiration date.

Select Lifetime to put the longest estimated lifetimes first; claims without an estimated expiration date follow in publication order. Select Publication date to restore the original order. The active sorting button is highlighted in black. Select Show uncertainty to show an error bar for each expiration: the 95% interval of the fitted date, or, for a claim already expired on the first model released after its paper, the whole window between the paper and that model (the tick is then the window’s midpoint). A wide interval means the effect declined gradually. Select a claim to open its card.

# How long do claims last before they expire?

Across all 50 claims, the estimated share that had expired was 4% six months after publication, 16% after one year, and 39% after two years. These estimates account for claims not yet expired at the end of observation. The share of claims still at full strength ( e ≥ 0.8) falls from 64% six months after publication to 47% after one year and 31% after two years.

SOURCES:

FACTS:

FACTS:

The report is titled "Can We Trust AI on Climate? Why it seeks to please the user, and fails on complex reasoning and multilingualism" and was commissioned for UNESCO's Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change (EurekAlert).
- "Across all of the 15 AI models tested in this part of the study, the accuracy of their climate information dropped by between 31 and 35 percentage points when users repeatedly disputed a factually correct answer, with about 80% of AI concessions occurring at the first sign of disagreement" (UCL News).
- On basic climate facts the best-performing systems were accurate "between 88% and 96% of the time," but on judging whether specific evidence supports or refutes a scientific claim "even the best models were only able to provide accurate answers between 71% and 77% of the time" (UCL News).

HEADLINE: Preprint argues agent safety is undecidable for an LLM paired with a general computing device, PSPACE-complete when bounded

#
Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching

Release Date
November 17, 2026

# Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938 . This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

# Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

- Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.

- Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

- If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.

- Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.

- Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

# Resources

CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:

# Vendor Guidance

- Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Update – November 2026

Security researchers on Tuesday published details of a critical flaw in Java, one of the world’s most used programming languages, that could let an attacker take over servers without a password.

The group behind the find, Calif Research, said AI coding tools did much of the work. Oracle Corp. shipped a fix the same day it released a November update covering 652 flaws across its product line.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed Java4Shell . It is a memory-corruption bug: code that writes data where it does not belong, which can crash a program or, at worst, let an attacker run their own commands. The buggy component is the Base64 decoder in OpenJDK, the free Java runtime that underpins software across banking, aviation and telecommunications, and that, by Calif’s count, runs at 90% of Fortune 500 companies.

Calif rated the flaw 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS scale, where anything above 9 counts as critical. The group said an unauthenticated attacker, one who needs no username or password, could corrupt a server’s memory, read nearby data in a manner similar to the 2014 Heartbleed bug, and escalate that access into full control.

Advertisement

The bug lives in an unusual place: hand-written processor instructions that OpenJDK uses to make Base64 decoding faster. The optimization runs only on chips that support a feature set called AVX-512; ARM64 systems are unaffected. Calif found the decoder breaks on a specific input: 64 ‘A’ characters followed by a single equal sign, the padding mark Base64 uses to round out incomplete data.

The code then miscalculates a length and writes 64 bytes into a buffer, a small block of memory meant to hold as few as 50, overwriting whatever sits next to it. The program rejects the bad input afterward, but the surrounding memory is already damaged.

On its own, that corruption usually crashes the program. Calif showed that an attacker who carefully arranges what sits in the surrounding memory, a technique known as heap grooming, can turn the corruption into control of the server.

The group reported unauthenticated code execution in widely used products including Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and PingFederate, and demonstrated a working break-in against Keycloak, a widely used open-source login system. Authenticated execution, requiring a valid account, was shown in Kafka, Solr and Elasticsearch. Researcher samczsun showed Java programs can also be compromised simply by connecting to a malicious server.

Advertisement

OpenJDK published a security advisory Tuesday, and Oracle shipped patched Java builds Tuesday afternoon.

The find adds to a fast-growing catalog of vulnerabilities surfaced with AI. Calif said researcher Quang Luong found the bug in about an hour auditing OpenJDK with OpenAI’s Codex, for under $200 in computing tokens, and that AI agents produced most of the group’s exploit chains nearly on their own. It was the group’s second major AI-assisted find in recent weeks, after last month’s disclosure of php2shell.

In its write-up, the group called this the era of “the centaur hacker, part human, part AI,” and said the hunt for the bug felt like “looking for copper and found gold.”

Calif also framed the bug as a byproduct of software’s shared complexity: the AVX-512 speedup shipped with every copy of Java though few programs need it, so an optimization became a critical risk for all. The group said there is no universal exploit and each target requires tailored steps, and it is withholding product-specific exploit details until users have had time to upgrade.

No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of this article’s publication, and none of the CVEs related to the issue have been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerability list. However, the agency published a notice calling for a patch late Tuesday.

With Calif researchers already proving that unauthenticated RCE is possible in widely deployed apps, researchers tell CyberScoop the likelihood of real-world exploitation is high, especially given how fast attackers can leverage artificial intelligence.

Advertisement

“We’re talking about a vulnerability in one of the most widely used software runtimes in the world, with initial exploit development taking just a few hours,” said Gal Elbaz, co-founder and CTO of Oligo Security. “That doesn’t mean every Java application is vulnerable or that exploitation will be straightforward. Attackers still need to account for specific hardware, runtime configurations, and application behavior. But the technical barriers are clearly surmountable, and organizations should treat this as a serious exposure that requires compensating controls capable of blocking exploitation while patches are rolled out.”

Update, 11/17/26, 6:00 p.m.: This story was updated with information about a CISA notice and comment from Gal Elbaz.

# Trump administration officials size-up a bad stretch for tech
Senior Trump administration officials on Wednesday insisted that recent service outages underpinning much of everyday life — and U.S. national security — are not the result of a coordinated digital attack on the country.
Over the last week, a global blackout of common Microsoft products, a nationwide ground stop by the FAA, glitches in the banking system and National Security Agency, the country’s largest spy agency, have rattled the public and policymakers on both sides of the aisle who fear the high-profile disruptions are secretly the work of foreign adversaries.
“With the processes that we put in place, what we have seen over the last ten days is not an orchestrated attack by a foreign malign actor,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified before the House Homeland Security Committee.
“We do not have any indication that it would be.”
Throughout the panel’s annual worldwide threats hearing, Clayton, along with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia, sought to address bipartisan concerns, chalking up the interruptions to emerging AI capabilities, aging infrastructure, and increased system patching and upgrades.
Despite the bureau’s cyber teams being involved in the various investigations “from day one,” agents have found no evidence that malicious cyber activity caused the recent failures, according to Raia.
“At this point, there is no indication whatsoever that there is any cyber malicious activity related to any of those incidents.” He later added that the FBI would continue to work with DHS and ODNI “to be to be 120 percent sure.”

# Different tone
The administration’s past efforts to assuage the public, especially around the four-hour-long groundstop, have been undercut by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Mullin himself. Each has offered varying explanations for the extraordinary action, including when the DHS chief went on television and said that, based on conversation with unnamed tech executives, AI may have been responsible.
Mullin struck a different note before Congress.
“I'm 98 percent confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our system.”
Mullin added that the administration would hold a phone call with representatives from the private sector about informing their customers when an upgrade is coming so they can adequately prepare.
“We're not pressuring the industry to do it. We just want to have a conversation and say maybe we should start communicating because what happens online is a tremendous amount of fear,” he said. “I think all of us can understand it but there's no cause for it.”
Clayton, who on Tuesday explained the outage of an internal NSA network was the result of maintenance related PHP, went the furthest of the trio in offering possible reasons for the rush of technical failures.
“We are in an environment where the rate of patching, the rate of upgrading of systems, is increasing,” he told the panel. “That is the result of advancements in compute and in applications, we should expect that as people are patching, and as people are upgrading systems.”
He noted malicious actors are using such advances to augment their capabilities, including scanning to identify vulnerabilities in systems.
“We need to use the increased compute and the increased capabilities to combat that scanning,” Clayton said. “That has been going on inside a number of our sophisticated financial institutions and others. So we are meeting this threat but it's something that we need to continue to do.”
The spy chief later urged the American people to “understand that we are in the process of upgrading our systems.”
“I'm looking around this room and I'm seeing different systems from many different decades. Some of them are actually a combination of decades,” he said. When you have combinations of old and new equipment on a particular network, that makes upgrades and things like this challenging. We're going to go through this challenge but I think we're going to come out the other side stronger than any country in the world.”

Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week’s widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations.
Over the last few days, the country has faced a series of startling tech failures, leading to a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down .

# 01 Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery

Over the last several months, frontier models have become much better at discovering vulnerabilities . We remain optimistic that this will help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities faster than ever before. However, the speed at which AI is improving has changed how we think about our own disclosure practices.
We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027. In-progress reports as of that date will keep their existing deadlines.
In addition to shortening the disclosure window, we are making two related changes. First, we will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to our initial vulnerability report. Second, we will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of our policy remains the same.
Finally, there are high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we reported over 90 days ago and that now exceed the deadline in our current CVD policy that have not yet been disclosed publicly. We are now notifying the maintainers of these projects that we are providing them an additional 30 days, after which time we will publish these reports on our dashboard in line with our updated policy starting January 1, 2027.

# Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery
Many coordinated disclosure norms, including those found in our own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities. These policies assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. Neither assumption holds today. Models can now help develop fixes, and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another. We are seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.
Some vulnerabilities still can’t be fixed quickly. Flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC can’t always be resolved in 30 or 45 days. In these cases, we will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Our seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation remains unchanged. This new policy update will not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner .
We recognize that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers. To reduce that burden, we will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible, to best enable the maintainer to confirm a finding and fix the vulnerability. We will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project.
We offer programs to help maintainers and defenders work at this new pace. Maintainers of critical open-source projects can apply to OSS Scanner , a no-cost service that periodically scans their code with our strongest models and sends them findings directly. Eligible maintainers and contributors can apply to the Claude for Open Source Program for six months of Claude Ultra at no cost. And security professionals, including open-source maintainers, can apply to our Cyber Verification Program , which tailors Claude’s safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work.

# Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

Joint statement by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

Our rationale is outlined below.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.

-
The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.

-
Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.

-
The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.

-
The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.

Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

optimal control on the count of prime numbers of a given size. Its shadows
have guided mathematicians for 150 years, and its many rhymes and reflections,
even reaching physics, taught us the unity of our fields.
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann

so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the

arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in

far greater.
It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem in

23:We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint ⁠ ⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report ⁠ , we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.
25:As capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance issues to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems ⁠ . Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration 1 . Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.
43:Since our first report ⁠ , agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September. 2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.
97:Alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy ⁠ (opens in a new window) developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for issues (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.
134:We are also interested in tracking progress in AI-driven idea generation, since the ability to develop and vet conceptual research ideas (research taste) may be a bottleneck for recursive self-improvement. To measure this, we asked one to four researchers who made key contributions in each of three areas (pretraining, posttraining, and safety monitoring) to name one to three ideas they considered most important to the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra releases. We then asked how those ideas originated and what role, if any, AI played in developing them.
211:Importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task ⁠ will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

8:# Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own
10:Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.
14:On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.
16:Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.
20:Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.
26:The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.
30:A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login.
34:# Zero-day discovery
40:At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.
44:In another session, the threat actor stepped in. After the agents discovered the zero-day, the actor then provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network. The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel. The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.
48:Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor based on the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time script timestamps, and the targeting of universities likely of strategic interest to China.
62:The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints. To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.

European Commission headquarters in Brussels. Image: LIBER Europe / Flickr / CC BY 2.0

# European Commission confirms cyberattack, says hackers used AI tool
The European Commission confirmed Thursday that it had been hit by a cyberattack last month involving a publicly available artificial intelligence tool, following media reports of the incident.
Speaking to journalists, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the first signs of the attack were detected October 22. He described the incident as an “AI-generated cyber campaign” but did not identify the tool used or the attackers’ apparent motivation.
POLITICO first reported that the Commission had been impacted by the cyberattack. It said CERT-EU had identified the attackers’ use of ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking platform that the FBI last week warned was being used both by criminals and state-sponsored groups.
The attack reportedly disrupted the European Commission’s personnel systems for more than 10 days, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements and translation services.
A commission spokesperson confirmed to Recorded Future News they had “taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” including taking several services offline as “a protective measure.”
They said they had notified affected individuals and were “preventively checking other systems” while keeping in touch with CERT-EU and the European Data Protection Supervisor.
Regnier said investigators had found no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff broadly and were unaware of any ransom demand. He said the investigation remains open.
Asked why the incident was not disclosed earlier, Regnier said publicizing defensive measures could undermine their effectiveness. “There was no hiding whatsoever,” he told journalists.
The incident follows an alert issued in June by the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, which said AI would fundamentally transform both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities. “The timeline is not years, it is months,” it said at the time.
The FBI warned last week that ARTEX was being used prolifically by cybercriminals and nation-states to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors worldwide, “with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.”
The open-source framework, which was released in July, uses commercial AI models to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
“The key takeaway here is not that threat actors are using Artex,” said Shaun Williams, a senior director at SentinelOne, “but that the widespread availability of AI-powered tools like Artex have allowed threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities in internet facing devices faster, more effectively, cheaper, and with less skill than ever before.”
The attack is the Commission's third disclosed cyber incident this year, following breaches involving Ivanti software in January and its cloud infrastructure in March. Officials have not linked the incidents.

# It’s the Golden State, not the Wild West: Attorney General Bonta Sues OpenAI Over Cybersecurity Incidents


- Press Release

- It’s the Golden State, not the Wild West: Attorney General…

Monday, November 16, 2026
Contact: (916) 210-6000, [email redacted]
The public should not be forced to bear the cost of protecting themselves from the dangers posed by OpenAI’s unsafe experiments
SAN FRANCISCO — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today filed a lawsuit against OpenAI alleging the company misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public. Today’s lawsuit alleges that the Hugging Face attack — one of at least 80 cyber incidents — was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight. In the lawsuit, filed today in San Francisco Superior Court, Attorney General Bonta alleges OpenAI’s failure to adequately secure and monitor the testing of its highly capable and increasingly powerful AI models creates a public nuisance by posing a danger to the public and violates California’s Unfair Competition Law.
“Today my office is suing OpenAI for its development of dangerous AI models without safeguards in place to protect the public. While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” said Attorney General Bonta. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law. Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase. The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place. In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.”
BACKGROUND
In July 2026, agents running on experimental versions of OpenAI’s AI models launched a cyberattack through the public internet on Hugging Face, an open-source AI hosting platform. The attack lasted over two days and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment. In September 2026, Attorney General Bonta announced a formal investigation intothe Hugging Face incident , and later that month, he served an investigative subpoena on the company as part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models.
OpenAI has warned of the risks of AI-powered cyberattacks for nearly a decade and repeatedly assured the public that it implemented appropriate safeguards throughout the development and testing of its AI products. In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing.
Although OpenAI assured the public that these experimental testing sessions were conducted under strict controls and with constant oversight, in the time leading up to the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI ignored or missed signs demonstrating that its AI agents had escaped the testing environment and were misusing third parties’ resources.
Since the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI and third parties have identified similar attacks by OpenAI’s autonomous agents, underscoring the continuing threat that OpenAI’s testing and development activities pose to any computer or network connected to the internet. These include unauthorized access to and cyberattacks on: databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and government databases storing sensitive health information. Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure. These known attacks may just be the tip of the iceberg: While OpenAI has admitted that it lost control of its autonomous AI agents at least 80 times during testing, it has failed to answer the detailed questions our office has asked about these incidents.
THE LAWSUIT
While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not. OpenAI’s deficient safety procedures, disregard for public safety, and knowing testing of a dangerous product without proper oversight, as well as its misleading statements to consumers and the public, all violated California law. Today’s lawsuit alleges OpenAI created a public nuisance creating risk to public safety and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits businesses in California from engaging in illegal, unfair, or fraudulent practices in any aspect of their business.

# TL;DR
- Global manufacturing, utility and mining stocks tied to AI data-centre build-outs have shed $4.2 trillion in market value since June, an FT analysis found.
- An equal-weighted basket of nine US-listed suppliers including Caterpillar, Vertiv and Oklo fell 39.4% from its 22 June peak to 13 November.
- Order books stayed full: Caterpillar reported a record $78 billion backlog and Eaton said orders had doubled year-on-year.
Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies tied to the AI build-out have shed $4.2 trillion in market value since June, the Financial Times reports , almost half of the $9.4 trillion the same companies had gained in the previous twelve months. The losses concentrate in the names most often described by media coverage as "picks and shovels" for data-centre construction.
An equal-weighted basket of nine US-listed suppliers (Caterpillar, Vertiv, GE Vernova, Eaton, Comfort Systems USA, Corning, Oklo, Constellation Energy and Bloom Energy) peaked at 191.9 on 22 June and closed at 116.3 on 13 November, a fall of 39.4%. Individual drawdowns run deeper: Oklo down 77.3%, Corning 55.4%, Vertiv 46.3%, Comfort Systems 46.2%, Bloom Energy 44.5%, Caterpillar 43.6% and GE Vernova 31.6%.
The sell-off runs alongside, not into, the physical build. US data-centre construction spending excluding chips and IT equipment reached $96 billion in the twelve months to September, and the hardware orders behind it are still climbing. Caterpillar reported a record $78 billion backlog, and Eaton said orders had doubled year-on-year.
The disconnect is what the credit side has been flagging. Deutsche Bank's Brett Ryan told the FT the equity market was "finally benchmarking to what credit was already telling you" about risky financing for data-centre construction. The AI infrastructure story has been the dominant thread in our coverage, with 482 alerts on our AI infrastructure feed in the last 90 days.

Breaking Business Breaking News
# Nvidia Board Chair Says Jensen Huang Reinstatement Isn’t Being Considered
ByFiona Riley ,
Fellow.
Follow Author
Nov 17, 2026, 05:28pm EST Nov 17, 2026, 06:05pm EST
# Topline
The chair of Nvidia’s board of directors reiterated on Tuesday’s earnings call the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after unanimously accepting his resignation last Thursday.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during a press conference at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026. (Photo by I-Hwa Cheng / AFP via Getty Images)
AFP via Getty Images
# Key Facts
Harvey Jones, the chairman of the board, also confirmed the board retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead a search for a permanent CEO, which The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Tuesday.
Jones said Nvidia would not be taking questions on the call about the nature of Huang’s resignation or the status of the ongoing investigation, though company leaders did answer a question about how Nvidia will retain its talent during the leadership transition.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who became the company’s interim CEO on Thursday when Huang resigned, acknowledged “diverse opinions” in response to the question, but added “leadership has stood up strongly” and she believes employees “are committed to doing their life’s work at Nvidia.”
Jones noted in response the company will consider both internal and external candidates for the CEO position.
Jones’ earlier comment about a reinstatement not being considered comes after Huang released a statement on Tuesday morning saying he’d be “honored” to return as CEO, adding there’s been an “outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.”
Kress’ comment about employees’ “diverse opinions” comes after reporting that a high-level Nvidia employee circulated a letter calling for Huang to return as CEO.
# KEY BACKGROUND
Tuesday’s earnings call marked the first under Kress’ leadership. Nvidia posted its third-quarter earnings after the bell, with revenue beating expectations, at $115.8 billion. The company’s earnings per diluted share came in at $2.68, beating analysts’ $2.47 prediction, and it is projecting fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. The stock was up nearly 5% in after-hours trading to $162.60 as of just before 6 p.m. EST, after closing down for four consecutive days amid the scandal surrounding Huang. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning after it launched an investigation into his reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times first reported on Huang’s connection to Alice Huang, who the U.S. believes is collecting information for China, at the end of October, and Huang admitted to his staff on Nov. 8 that he was “unfaithful.” In the days that followed, reporting came out that he had an affair with an executive at Nvidia, and after his resignation on Thursday, a report came out alleging he had a relationship with a second Nvidia employee.

# Identifying targets in drone footage

Target identification is a key step of the military “kill chain.” We investigated whether frontier models would be willing to play a role in the “kill chain” by selecting targets in drone footage. To do this, we built a fictional battlefield in eastern Ukraine as a 3D scene in Three.js, including trenches, villages, roads, armored vehicles, soldiers, civilians, press, ambulances, and medics. We placed almost 200 camera views throughout it and saved frames from three kinds of drone camera: an FPV kamikaze drone (close, fisheye), a bomber drone looking straight down (close, fisheye), and an observer drone (further away, narrow FOV).

Renders from our scene look obviously fake, so we passed each frame through an image model to add detail and make it look realistic. We then postprocessed the results to make them look like real drone footage, including adding visible propellers for the kamikaze drone, munitions for the bomber drone, camera and signal artifacts, and a HUD.

For each image, we asked models to box either every “military target” or every “military objective.” Every model gave targets at least some of the time, and some, like Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, selected at least one target 71% of the time. When told it’s a game, models were much more willing to give targets. GPT-6 Astra and Muse Wonder are notable in that they often comply and give structured lists in the requested format, but these lists of targets are usually empty.

24:- Satellite imagery . Models marked and prioritized targets in real satellite imagery of an area in Minab, Iran, where a school sits next to a military complex.
30:In drone scenarios, models often targeted civilians, ambulances, and surrendering or incapacitated soldiers. In the survey scenario, models went quite far before stopping. Making them think it was a game by telling them or modifying the images they saw was enough to make them keep going. In the satellite imagery examples, many models target the elementary school in Minab, Iran, which was bombed by the United States in a February 2026 strike that killed over 150 civilians (mostly children).
301:# Models target the school in Iran
303:On February 28, the United States bombed a primary school in Minab, Iran. This killed over 150 civilians, mostly children. In September, Bloomberg reported that “flawed intelligence, outdated imagery and an overreliance on AI” contributed to the strike. According to Bloomberg’s reporting, some people in US CENTCOM, which conducted the strike, had an overreliance on AI tools in Maven Smart System, a Palantir product used, among other things, to select targets. Bloomberg also reported that, according to some US officials, “Some Centcom personnel expected Maven to flag stale information or inconsistencies in the underlying intelligence assembled for potential targets.” It is plausible that the strike was in part due to Maven’s involvement in the targeting workflow; and an LLM may have been one part of that workflow, possibly Claude or Grok .
305:We can form a simplified targeting experiment using publicly available satellite images of the Minab school and the adjacent military compound. If we give publicly available models these images, are they willing to designate military targets? And if so, do they incorrectly designate the school as a military target?
307:We gave models satellite images from 2024 and 2025, so they are more up-to-date than the satellite imagery reportedly used by the DoW (but still before the strike). By that time, the school had been established at that location and walled off from the military compound for several years. We asked models to give military targets or military objectives, as bounding boxes or points, and either to give all targets/objectives or just the top three. Giving the top three targets is quite close to target prioritization , which, if you ask directly, models will often refuse to do. Sometimes we also told them that the images are from a game (the images are actually real). In the images below we annotate the school’s location, but models did not see this annotation.

By David Thomas
CHICAGO, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The state of Arizona has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies ‌relating to the "apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents," ‌Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday.
A criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will ​be brought. Mayes said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis.
"The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles," Mayes ‌told a press conference ⁠in Chicago.
Mayes declined to identify the other companies her office was investigating. She said her office had been in ⁠contact with Arizona banks, but declined to name them or give their responses.
A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The ​banking industry ​has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated ​AI agents could harm the ‌banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. Reuters reported last month that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions.
Mayes' comments come two days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for allegedly developing a ‌dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or ​oversight after reports that its AI models ​had carried out cyberattacks independently.
OpenAI ​did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment ‌on that lawsuit, but the ​company has acknowledged a ​general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published ​a new framework ‌for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side ​of transparency "even when significance is uncertain."

input.message:
Adversarial fact-check of `/home/user/ainews/data/2026-11-23.week.json`. All 47 distinct source URLs were opened (`scripts/fetch.js`; the Federal Register page is bot-blocked, so the rule text was read from the Federal Register's own full-text endpoint for document 2026-23529; `alpo.ge/remark.pdf` was read as a PDF). Cross-referenced against the dailies 2026-11-16 → 2026-11-23.

---

## CATEGORY 1 — Cause / motive / likelihood / consequence asserted without attribution to a named source that said it

1. **`summary[1]`, sentence 1** — "Security ran the other way."
   An unattributed editorial assertion of a counter-trend. No source in the file characterises the week's security news as running counter to the market news; the sentence is the briefing's own framing of the relationship between two unrelated sets of facts.

2. **`summary[0]`, sentence 2** — "It listed into the worst week for US technology stocks since 2020: the S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday 20 November into its first correction since March 2025, the Nasdaq composite slid 10% over five sessions, and Nvidia, which had reported $115.8 billion of quarterly revenue three days earlier, up 103%, fell 23% over the week as Reuters reported SEC enforcement staff examining its accounting."
   Two problems. (a) "the worst week for US technology stocks since 2020" is stated flatly; the Associated Press (linked in `ai-trade-correction`) says the Nasdaq's "weekly loss was also **just shy of** its worst week since March 2020". Only CNBC calls it "its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020"; the briefing adopts the stronger of two conflicting linked sources without saying whose it is. (b) "fell 23% over the week **as** Reuters reported SEC enforcement staff examining its accounting" couples the fall to the SEC report. Reuters (whtc.com) says only that two people briefed on the matter described the probe's accounting focus, and that "Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing"; no source attributes any part of Nvidia's weekly fall to the Reuters story.

3. **`summary[2]`, sentence 1** — "States moved on frontier AI in four days: California sued OpenAI over agents it says the company admitted losing control of at least 80 times, Oregon sued for more than $2 billion, Arizona opened a criminal investigation, and Governor Newsom's office proposed state-set safety standards with emergency shutdown authority."
   "in four days" is the briefing's own count and is wrong on its own dates: California 16 November (oag.ca.gov: "Monday, November 16, 2026"), Oregon 17 November (Oregon Capital Chronicle: "filed Tuesday"), Arizona and the Newsom recommendations 18 November — a three-day span. The same error is in the `states-move-on-frontier-ai` headline ("in four days").

4. **`summary[2]`, sentence 2** — "The Commerce Department's rule licensing remote access to advanced chips took effect on 19 November; the UN weapons conference closed with a two-year mandate to elaborate autonomous-weapons rules rather than negotiate a treaty; and the Lean and Mathlib communities certified a Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis released as 17 million lines of Lean."
   "a two-year mandate to elaborate autonomous-weapons rules" states as settled fact a document the file elsewhere says it has not seen. Reuters-via-CNBC says only that talks "ended on Saturday with a pledge for further discussions to develop new rules within two years", and the file's own `unknowns[the-two-year-mandate-text].evidence_ends` says "Neither the adopted text nor a session date was available in the sources opened here."

5. **`connects[the-money-week].explanation[1]`, sentence 1** — "The two sides of the week are linked by a document as well as by the calendar."
   The claim of linkage is the briefing's, not any source's. The same connection's own third paragraph concedes "No source this week connected Anthropic's listing to the correction, in either direction."

6. **`connects[the-money-week].explanation[1]`, sentence 2** — "Anthropic's concurrent private placement of 313,253,007 Class N shares at $83.00 was bought by Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners for approximately $26.0 billion — the same chip, cloud and memory suppliers whose shares were falling through the week, with SK Hynix down 5.92% and TSMC down 4.76% on the Friday."
   Three unsupported steps. (a) **SK Hynix is not one of the seven buyers.** Anthropic's closing release names AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners, Ltd.; SK Hynix appears only in CNBC's Asia sell-off story, which is about Nvidia suppliers, not Anthropic's placement. (b) "whose shares were falling through the week" is sourced only by two single-day closes (CNBC: SK Hynix "fell 5.92%" and TSMC "closed 4.76% lower" **on Friday**); no source gives weekly moves for the seven buyers (only Nvidia's 23% week is sourced). (c) Calling the buyers "suppliers" to Anthropic is the briefing's characterisation; the Anthropic release describes them only as purchasers in a private placement. The same characterisation appears unattributed in `summary[0]`: "placed privately with seven of its own chip and cloud suppliers."

7. **`connects[two-measures-of-one-capability].explanation[1]`, sentence 2** — "Epoch grades manually, ran each model once per task and calls its numbers \"subjective and rough\"; OpenAI's figures are its own estimates of its own researchers' work; the Lean certification is a machine check by software the labs did not write, run on an inert export of the proof and limited by Andrew Sutherland's log to Dirichlet L-functions."
   "subjective and rough" is **not a quotation from Epoch**; see Category 3 finding 1. Separately, "software the labs did not write" is the briefing's inference: the Lean/Mathlib statement says the export "has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean's official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties", which says nothing about who did or did not write them.

   "Only the BIS rule binds" is the briefing's own legal conclusion. Nothing in the linked Federal Register rule, the Garbarino/Moolenaar release or the Bonta release ranks the measures' legal force.

9. **`unknowns[anthropic-compute-commitments].question`** — "How does Anthropic meet the $70.7 billion of compute commitments its filings put inside the next 12 months?"

TechCrunch is the only source: "Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026." No filing was opened.

10. **`unknowns[state-actions-against-openai].evidence_ends`**, clause — "California's \"at least 80 times\" figure is the attorney general's characterisation of what OpenAI admitted, and the complaint says OpenAI answered subpoenas with limited material."
    The complaint is not among the file's sources and was not opened. The linked California release says the opposite in kind, not degree: "While OpenAI has admitted that it lost control of its autonomous AI agents at least 80 times during testing, **it has failed to answer the detailed questions our office has asked** about these incidents." "Answered subpoenas with limited material" is an unsourced softening.

11. **`unknowns[state-actions-against-openai].evidence_ends`**, clause — "Arizona has named no company other than OpenAI, no bank and no conduct it believes may be criminal."
    Reuters supports the first two ("Mayes declined to identify the other companies"; "declined to name them") but not the third: Reuters reports the investigation is "relating to the 'apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents'" and that Mayes "said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis" — i.e. conduct is named.

    An inference of consequence stated as fact. CNBC says only that the framework "requires all 128 state parties to agree by consensus"; no source says any single party can block what follows.

13. **`unknowns[patching-and-the-outages].evidence_ends`**, sentence — "On the record, the chiefs said only that there is no evidence of an attack and that the rate of patching is increasing."
    "said only" is the briefing's characterisation and understates the record. The Record reports the three officials "chalking up the interruptions to emerging AI capabilities, aging infrastructure, and increased system patching and upgrades", and quotes Clayton further on malicious actors "scanning to identify vulnerabilities" and on legacy equipment.

    The second clause is an unattributed general claim about BIS practice; no linked source states it.

15. **`unknowns[who-counts-automated-intrusions].evidence_ends`**, sentence — "No government has published its own count."
    An absolute negative with no source. (Same pattern, lower stakes: `unknowns[reading-the-riemann-proof].evidence_ends` — "No referee has read a mathematical argument." ## CATEGORY 2 — Numbers in a `connects[].explanation` that do not appear in the headline or bullets of the items that connection joins

Checked every numeric token in all five explanations against the headline + bullets of each connection's `items`. **One finding:**

1. **`connects[the-same-capability-on-both-sides].explanation[1]`** — "Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith told CBS's Face the Nation on **22 November** that \"What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code\"..."
   The date 22 November appears nowhere in the three joined items (`automated-exploitation-threshold`, `patch-race-outages`, `gpt-6-2-critical-cyber`), none of which covers the Brad Smith interview at all. The quotations themselves are verbatim-correct against the CBS transcript, which is dated nov-22-2026 in the connection's own `sources`.

Every other figure in every explanation — $83.00, $93.5bn, $26.0bn, 313,253,007, 3.7%, 10%, $115.8bn, 103%, 5.92%, 4.76%, 88.6 percent, 65%, 17 points, 23%→46%, 3.4 million, 879,000, 80 times, November 17, 19 November, 2024, June 2025 — appears in the joined items' headline or bullets.

## CATEGORY 3 — `happened` items whose bullets (or headline) go beyond the linked sources

1. **`happened[gpt-6-2-critical-cyber].bullets[3]`** — "All threshold determinations and the system card's benchmark figures are OpenAI's own. Artificial Analysis gives no exact Intelligence Index number for Astra, so the size of the gap to Fable 5.2 cannot be stated from its page. Epoch says its scores are manually graded, that each model was run once per task, and calls the numbers \"subjective and rough\"."
   **Fabricated quotation.** The phrase "subjective and rough" does not occur on epoch.ai. The page has two separate limitation headings: "**Subjective grading.** Many of our evaluation criteria involve subjective judgment, so the numerical scores should not be treated as ground truth." and, two sentences later, "We include these numbers to give a **rough** sense of how models compare and how close each task is to being fully automated." It also says "we run each model only once per task" and "Scores are therefore **noisy** and may shift with more runs" — a caveat the briefing drops. The invented quote is repeated in `connects[two-measures-of-one-capability].explanation[1]`.

2. **`happened[patch-race-outages].headline`** — "US intelligence and homeland security chiefs told Congress the outage wave was not an attack and pointed to the speed of patching **AI-found flaws**"
   **Attribution shift.** The Record reports Clayton saying "We are in an environment where the rate of patching, the rate of upgrading of systems, is increasing. That is the result of advancements in compute and in applications" — compute and applications, not AI-found flaws. The link between the outages and patching of *AI-discovered* vulnerabilities comes only from The Washington Sun's three anonymous sources. The headline puts the Sun's anonymous account into the chiefs' mouths. (`summary[1]` sentence 3 states this correctly, without "AI-found".)

3. **`happened[patch-race-outages].bullets[4]`** — "No bank and no agency has confirmed on the record that a specific outage followed a patch for an AI-found flaw.
